title: Keiran Suchak
text:
I am a Research Fellow in Mobility Data Science in the School of Geography at the University of Leeds. Within the school, I am a member of the Institute for Spatial Data Science and the Mobility Science Lab.
My current research focuses on exploring the mobility of healthcare workers and its impact on the way in which infections spread within healthcare settings; this research forms part of a broader digital health hub focused on antimicrobial resistance.
I previously did my PhD at the Leeds Institute for Data Analytics, working on the development of novel methods for the real-time simulation of pedestrian systems. During my PhD, I also held the role of Data Science Fellow with the Connected Places Catapult, working on modelling and mapping the incidence of social isolation.

title: Agent-based models of the United States wealth distribution with Ensemble Kalman Filter
text: The distribution of wealth is central to economic, social, and environmental dynamics. The release of high-frequency distributional data and the rapid pace of the complex global economy makes ‘real-time’ predictions about the distribution of wealth and income increasingly relevant. For instance, during the COVID-19 pandemic in spring 2020, the stock markets experienced a crash followed by a surge within a brief period, evidently reshaping the wealth distribution in the US. Yet economic data, when first released, can be uncertain and need to be readjusted — again specifically so during crisis moments like the pandemic when information about household consumption and business returns is patchy and drastically different from “business-as-usual”. Our motivation here is to develop one way of overcoming the problem of uncertain ‘real-time’ data and enable economic simulation methods, such as agent-based models, to accurately predict in ‘real-time’ when combined with newly released data. Therefore, we tested two distinct, parsimonious agent-based models of wealth distribution, calibrated with US data from 1990 to 2022, in conjunction with data assimilation. Data assimilation is essentially applied control theory — a set of algorithms aiming to improve model predictions by integrating ‘real-time’ observational data into a simulation. The algorithm we employed is the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF), which performs well in the context of computationally expensive problems. Our findings reveal that while the base models already align well historically, the EnKF enables a superior fit to the data.

title: An agent-based model of the 2020 international policy diffusion in response to the COVID-19 pandemic with particle filter
text: Global problems, such as pandemics and climate change, require rapid international coordination and diffusion of policy. These phenomena are rare however, with one notable example being the international policy response to the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020. Here we build an agent-based model of this rapid policy diffusion, where countries constitute the agents and with the principal mechanism for diffusion being peer mimicry. Since it is challenging to predict accurately the policy diffusion curve, we utilize data assimilation, that is an “on-line” feed of data to constrain the model against observations. The specific data assimilation algorithm we apply is a particle filter because of its convenient implementation, its ability to handle categorical variables and because the model is not overly computationally expensive, hence a more efficient algorithm is not required. We find that the model alone is able to predict the policy diffusion relatively well with an ensemble of at least 100 simulation runs. The particle filter however improves the fit to the data, reliably so from 500 runs upwards, and increasing filtering frequency results in improved prediction.

title: Exploring the impact of driver adherence to speed limits and the interdependence of roadside collisions in an urban environment: an agent-based modelling approach
text: Roadside collisions are a significant problem faced by all countries. Urbanisation has led to an increase in traffic congestion and roadside vehicle collisions. According to the UK Government’s Department for Transport, most vehicle collisions occur on urban roads, with empirical evidence showing drivers are more likely to break local and fixed speed limits in urban environments. Analysis conducted by the Department for Transport found that the UK’s accident prevention measure’s cost is estimated to be £33bn per year. Therefore, there is a strong motivation to investigate the causes of roadside collisions in urban environments to better prepare traffic management, support local council policies, and ultimately reduce collision rates. This study utilises agent-based modelling as a tool to plan, experiment and investigate the relationship between speeding and vehicle density with collisions. The study found that higher traffic density results in more vehicles travelling at a slower speed, regardless of the degree to which drivers comply with speed restrictions. Secondly, collisions increase linearly as speed compliance is reduced for all densities. Collisions are lowest when all vehicles comply with speed limits for all densities. Lastly, higher global traffic densities result in higher local traffic densities near-collision sites across all adherence levels, increasing the likelihood of congestion around these sites. This work, when extended to real-world applications using empirical data, can support effective road safety policies.

title: Influencing transport-health interactions through incentivised mode switch using new data and models
text:
In this study we present a ‘proof-of-concept’ model using novel model integration and new forms of data that addresses the research question, How does incentivising a change in travel mode to reduce personal car use impact health? We focus on simple transport-health interactions between switching between car and bus: the exposure to activity and pollution linked to these modes and how these changes effect health status, which in turn influences the mode choice.
We identify a basic causal loop diagram of key conceptual feedback between mode choice and health status (related to exposure to activity and pollution). From this we build a simple system dynamics stock and flow simulation model, with data input from spatial micro-simulation synthetic populations derived from ‘track and trace’ data as the output from an agent-based model. We then analyse scenarios of mode shift incentivised by bus fare reduction and bus frequency increase.
In the tested scenarios of this novel modelling approach, we identify that a reduction in bus fare or increase in bus frequency could incentivise a shift from car to bus which would result in a small decrease in relative risk of all causes mortality. Reducing bus fare in particular could provide both health and financial benefits for the most deprived communities.
This modelling approach presented in this data is a promising new method for the study of complex transport-health interactions. From our prototype model we have identified the impacts of mode shift on health status through exposure to pollution and activity, using unique feedbacks that are unaccounted for in conventional models.

title: Deep Vents
text:
Deep Vents is a 2-4 player ecosystem-building game. Grow archaea on connected hexes, convert it to the personal supply that scores, and use triggers to build shells or attack rival ecosystems. After eight turns each, the richest surviving ecosystem wins.



Adjacent heat, rock, bioluminescence, and predation traits power many growth effects.
Archaea on a hex are productive but score only half as efficiently as archaea in personal supply.
Attacks drain personal supply, so shells and avoiding shortfall matter as much as growth.

title: Deep Vents
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Give each player one Deep Vent starting hex; return unused starting hexes to the box in a 2- or 3-player game. Shuffle the remaining hexes face-up as a central stack and reveal the top five in a row to its left. The display therefore has six available hexes including the top of the stack.

Table checklist

Choose a first player, then give starting archaea by player count and seat: 2 players receive 10 and 11; 3 players receive 15, 16, and 17; 4 players receive 20, 21, 22, and 23.
Put all remaining archaea and shells in the general supply.
Keep shortfall tokens and the two track cubes available for hexes that use tracks.

title: Deep Vents
text:
Rounds and Phases
Players take eight turns each, clockwise. A turn is choose, place, activate, then refill. Hexes retain any archaea already on them when taken, and no hex may hold more than ten; excess is lost.

Teaching a placement

Choose a display hex. The leftmost is free; for any later hex, place one archaeon from personal supply on every skipped hex, left to right.
Add it adjacent by at least one side to your ecosystem.
Activate every hex in your ecosystem once, in top-left to bottom-right order. For each, choose grow or trigger, never both, and do not return to a previous hex. Grow adds archaea from supply according to its symbols, commonly one per matching adjacent passive trait. A trigger pays its listed cost from that hex or collects/uses its stated effect; repeat a trigger as often as affordable before continuing. If triggering would have no effect, grow instead.
Slide unclaimed hexes left and replenish from the stack; play passes left.



Important exception
Attacks remove archaea from every opponent’s personal supply, sometimes once per matching trait in their ecosystem. A defender may spend one shell per attack to block half the damage, rounded up. If damage exceeds a player’s supply, they take a shortfall token and 10 archaea, then finish taking the damage. A player with a shortfall at the start of their turn must take the leftmost hex; end a turn with two shortfalls and be eliminated. A shortfall can be repaid at any time for 10 personal archaea.

title: Deep Vents
text:
Scoring
The game ends after all players have completed eight turns, when each has nine hexes, or immediately once all but one player has been eliminated. Score 1 point per personal archaeon, 1 per two unused shells rounded up, 1 per two archaea on your hexes rounded up, and subtract 10 per shortfall token. Highest score wins; ties go to the player earlier in turn order.

Endgame
Decimated hexes are flipped in place: take half their archaea, rounded up, into personal supply, return the rest, and thereafter use only their reverse-side passive trait. They cannot be grown or triggered, but may still receive archaea from adjacent effects.

title: Deep Vents
text:
Terminology

Grow: Add archaea from the general supply to the active hex.
Trigger: Pay or collect archaea to resolve a hex’s upper-left action.
Personal supply: Your scored archaea, and the pool damaged by attacks.
Shell: A one-attack defence token.
Shortfall: Borrowed archaea after over-damage, worth -10 points.

title: Chai Garam
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
For the Basic Game, prepare the customer deck by placing the Evening Customer face-down between two roughly equal halves of the shuffled remaining customers. Remove one Water card per player from the Basics deck for starting supplies, remove Pakora snacks, and remove the zero-cost medium saucepans for players. Make three face-up cards for each of the Tea Leaf, Basics, and Additives markets; the Snacks deck stays face-down.

Table checklist

Shuffle the Goal deck and reveal 3 Public Goals for 2-3 players or 4 for 4 players. Deal 9 customers into the Mela’s 3 by 3 grid.
Put coins, half-star tokens, negative tokens, Chai Garam cards, and the three face-up saucepan piles within reach.
Give every player a Tapri, Basic upgrade board, 12 cups, 3 upgrade tokens, one zero-cost medium saucepan, one reserved Water, one Chai Garam card, one personal Goal, and a reference card.
The most recent tea drinker is first player. The second player draws a Tea Leaf; the third draws a Tea Leaf and Additive; the fourth also draws a Basics card.

title: Chai Garam
text:
Rounds and Phases
Turns proceed clockwise. On your turn take one main action, any number of free actions, and at most one Chai Garam card. You may hold at most two Chai Garam cards. A Pick action takes up to three market cards, with no more than one face-down Snack; immediately refill each face-up ingredient taken. Ingredients are hidden and the hand limit is nine, checked after picking.

Turn sequence

Use free actions before, between, or after main actions. Prepare chai by putting an entire recipe, plus optional additives, into one saucepan, then immediately add cup tokens equal to its size. Ingredients cannot be changed once cups are placed; discard them when its final cup is served.
Pick ingredients or take a Serve action. To serve, have at least one cup of the matching chai type ready and choose one row or one column of the Mela; serve one to three customers in it, skipping is allowed.
For each served customer choose simple or specific service and partial or complete fulfilment. Simple service needs only the chai type and pays 1 rupee per black/green cup or 2 per milk cup. Specific service matches the listed type, leaf, and additives, pays the printed amount, and earns a half-star from a celebrity or critic if completely served.
Add negative tokens to every unserved customer to the left of any served customer in that row. Each such customer loses 1 rupee per cup per token; discard one whose tolerance is reached. If you disgruntled anyone, take one negative token yourself.
Take payment, then a receipt only if you alone supplied every cup; otherwise discard the completed customer. Return cups and negatives, slide each row left, and refill it to nine customers. Serving at least one cup to three Mela customers in one row or column on a turn gains a Chai Garam card.



Useful reminder
Claim a completed Public or Personal Goal as a free action for a half-star; receipts spent for goals are discarded. Refill a claimed Public Goal, or draw a new Personal Goal, at turn end. Each pair of half-stars immediately unlocks one upgrade. Once per turn, you may buy a saucepan into an empty one of your three slots; emptying one wastes its chai and gives you one negative token per cup.

title: Chai Garam
text:
Scoring
End the game at the end of the turn in which a player reaches four full stars, serves the Evening Customer, or causes that customer to leave through intolerance. Score 1 point per full star and 0.5 per half-star, 0.5 per complete 10 rupees after resolving your negative tokens, 0.5 per six unused receipts, and 0.5 per six unserved chai cups. The highest total wins; break a tie with the higher star rating, then share victory.

Endgame
The Advanced Game, Kadak Chai, changes the target to five full stars and adds customer tags, the Funfair bonus track, specialisations, and personal queues. This teach uses the Basic Game; do not mix those advanced rules into it.

title: Chai Garam
text:
Terminology

Mela: The shared customer grid; service is restricted to one row or column.
Specific service: A cup matching all of a customer’s stated requirements.
Negative token: A penalty that reduces a customer’s payment and counts towards their tolerance.
Receipt: A completely fulfilled customer claimed by a single player.
Chai Garam card: A card discarded for an extra main action or to clear negatives from declared customer orders.

First player:

title: Evolution: Another World
text:
Rounds and Phases

The game comprises of several rounds.
Each round, players take turns clockwise.
At the start of the round, each player may redraw cards once; when redrawing, players discard their hand and redraw an each number of cards from the Evolution deck.
If the deck runs out of cards, immediately shuffle the discard pile to form a new deck.
The round ends as soon as all creatures of all players are asleep, i.e. have gained a Sleep token.
A turn comprises of players taking the following actions:

Create a new creature: Place 1 Evolution card face down from your hand to the table, creating a new creature with no traits (optional).
Add a new trait: Place 1 Evolution card from your hand face up under one of your exiting creatures, providing the trait to the creature (optional).
Activate: Choose 1 of your non-sleeping creatures and activate it (compulsory).



Notes

Creating creatures:

You may create as many creatures as you want over the course of the game.
The creatures of a player are considered friendly to each other; friendly creatures can attach each other.
Creatures do not die.

Adding traits:

You may add a trait to sleeping creatures.
A creature can have multiple different traits but can never have more than one copy of a trait.

Activating traits:

After activating a creature’s traits, it must perform one of the following actions:

Gain energy,

title: The Crew: Quest for Planet Nine
text:
The Crew is a cooperative campaign of 50 trick-taking missions for 3-5 players; a two-player variant uses the simulated third player JARVIS. The crew must make the right player win each required card, usually without discussing the cards in their hands.


Most missions assign coloured-card tasks. A task is complete when its owner wins a trick containing the matching playing card. The mission logbook sets the number of tasks, any task order, and any special rule; play the missions in order for the campaign.

Prepare a mission

Choose the mission and read its instructions. Shuffle the 40 playing cards and deal them as evenly as possible. With three players, one card is left unplayed after the final trick.
Give each player a communication token green-side up and a reminder card. Put the distress-signal token inactive, shuffle the task cards face down, and keep task tokens available.
If the mission uses task cards, place the specified number face up. The holder of the 4 rocket becomes Commander, takes the Commander token, and chooses first; players then take tasks clockwise until they are all assigned. Take any attached task token with its task.
If the mission specifies task tokens, lay them out first and place task cards against them from left to right. The token’s condition travels with the task when it is chosen.
After task distribution but before any communication, the crew may activate a distress signal. Everyone passes one non-rocket card to the adjacent player in one agreed direction. The signal remains active for every retry of that mission, and adds one to the logged attempt total on success.



Two players
Set the rockets aside. Make JARVIS from seven face-down cards with seven face-up cards directly over them, then shuffle the rockets into the remaining cards and deal 13 cards to each player. JARVIS counts as a third crew member. The Commander chooses JARVIS’s tasks and plays one of its face-up cards on its turns without discussion; reveal the card beneath only after the trick ends.

title: The Crew: Quest for Planet Nine
text:
Rounds and Phases

Play a trick

The Commander leads the first trick; thereafter, the previous trick winner leads. The leader may play any card, which establishes the suit, including a rocket.
In clockwise order, each other player must follow that suit if able. If unable, they may play any card. There is never an obligation to play a winning card.
The highest card in the led colour wins unless a rocket was played. Rockets are trump; if rockets are led, they must be followed where possible, and the highest rocket wins.
The winner keeps the trick face down, checks whether tasks in it were completed, and leads next. Only the most recently won trick may be inspected.



Communicate once
After tasks have been distributed and before, never during, a trick, a player may communicate once per mission attempt. Place one coloured card face up and put the token at its top, middle, or bottom to mean respectively that it is the highest, only, or lowest card of that colour in hand. Rockets cannot be communicated. The card remains playable; when played, discard the reminder card and turn the token red. Its stated position cannot later be changed.


Mission procedures
The logbook can override the normal task distribution or communication rules. Number tokens require tasks to be completed in that sequence; arrow tokens require only their linked precedence. Several tasks won in one trick are valid only when their order tokens are consecutive.
A dead zone permits a communication card without its positional token. A disruption forbids communication until the named trick. A Commander’s decision has the Commander ask each other player only “yes” or “no”, then assign all face-down tasks to one of them. A Commander’s distribution similarly uses yes/no responses, but the Commander assigns each revealed task and final task counts may differ by no more than one.

title: The Crew: Quest for Planet Nine
text:
Scoring

Succeed or fail
There are no victory points. The crew wins immediately when every required task has been completed and every mission condition met. It loses immediately if a player wins a card matching another player’s task, violates a task order, or breaks a mission-specific rule. Reshuffle, redeal, and draw new tasks to retry.
Record the number of attempts after a successful mission. If the distress signal was activated, add one to that number. Completing all 50 missions completes the campaign.

title: The Crew: Quest for Planet Nine
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Trick: one card played by every crew member.
Lead suit: the colour or rocket suit set by the first card in a trick.
Rocket: a trump card, valued 1-4.
Commander: the holder of the 4 rocket, who starts task selection and the first trick.
Task: a playing card that its task-card owner must win.
Communication token: the once-per-attempt signal for a highest, only, or lowest coloured card.
Distress signal: an optional pre-mission card pass that increases the recorded attempts by one.

title: Star Trek: Missions
text:
Build the highest-scoring seven-card hand from Galaxy and Mission cards. Galaxy cards are the characters, places, equipment, and artefacts that supply attributes and bonuses; Mission cards are scoring challenges. Everything is evaluated only against cards in your own final hand.

A card that is blanked scores no points, grants no points, and has no effect, but still occupies one of your seven hand slots.

title: Star Trek: Missions

title: Star Trek: Missions
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Shuffle the 50-card Galaxy deck and 24-card Mission deck separately. Deal every player five Galaxy cards and two Mission cards. Put both decks facedown beside a shared, initially empty discard area; choose a starting player at random and play clockwise.

Table checklist

Keep the Galaxy and Mission decks separate throughout the game.
Spread all discarded cards face up so every player can inspect the whole discard area, not just its most recent card.
Each player begins with seven cards and two Missions. The score pad is needed only after the end trigger.

title: Star Trek: Missions
text:
Rounds and Phases
There are no rounds or phases: players take one turn at a time until the shared discard area contains either eight Galaxy cards or twelve Mission cards. A turn always ends with seven cards in hand and one or two Mission cards.

Turn sequence

Choose exactly one option: take one card from the discard area, then discard a different card; draw the top Galaxy card, then discard any card; or draw the top two Mission cards, then discard any two cards.
Discards go face up into the shared discard area. The cards taken from it can be Galaxy or Mission cards.
Check your Mission count after discarding. You may not end with zero Missions or with more than two.
The game ends immediately once the discard area reaches eight Galaxy cards or twelve Mission cards. Finish the current turn’s required discards before scoring.



Reading card text

WITH grants the bonus once if at least one named card or attribute is present.
FOR EACH grants the stated bonus once for every qualifying card.
A single card may grant bonuses to several cards, but it cannot grant the same receiving card more than one bonus, even if it matches several requested criteria.
Resolve BLANKS and BLANKED UNLESS WITH first. A blanked card cannot score, give bonuses, or affect the hand in any way.

title: Star Trek: Missions
text:
Scoring
At game end, score every non-blanked card in each player’s seven-card hand, including Mission cards, according to its text and the other cards in that hand. Do not compare or combine players’ hands.

Scoring order

Identify cards blanked outright or blanked unless their stated condition is present.
Ignore those cards completely, except that they still count towards the seven-card hand size.
Add the values and conditional bonuses of every remaining Galaxy and Mission card, applying the one-bonus-per-giving-card restriction.
The highest total wins; tied players share victory.

title: Star Trek: Missions
text:
Terminology

Galaxy card: A card with attributes and scoring text.
Mission card: A text-only card that scores as part of the final hand.
Type, Specialty, Lifeform, Affiliation: Galaxy-card attributes that card text can require or reward.
Blanked: A card that neither scores nor has any effect, while still taking a hand slot.
With / For Each: Respectively, a one-off conditional bonus and a bonus repeated for each qualifying card.

title: Drinking Fluxx
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Deal the game

Shuffle all cards and deal three to each player.
Put the rest face-down as a draw pile, with space for discards.
Choose a first player.
Start with no Goal, no Keepers, and the Basic Rule Draw 1, Play 1.

If the draw pile is empty, shuffle the discard pile into a new draw pile. Cards in play are never shuffled back in.

title: Drinking Fluxx
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take a turn

Draw the number required by the active Draw rule.
Play the number required by the active Play rule.
Resolve every card as it is played.
Discard down to active Hand and Keeper Limits after playing.
Check the current Goal before play passes clockwise.



Card effects

Keepers stay in front of their owner and can satisfy Goals.
A Goal or New Rule replaces the previous card of that type.
An Action resolves once, then is discarded.
A Creeper stays in play and normally prevents its owner from winning unless a Goal says otherwise.
A Surprise can be played only at the timing printed on it, sometimes outside your turn.

New Rules can change draw, play, hand, or Keeper limits immediately. Do as much of an impossible instruction as you can. Specific card text overrides the general rules.

title: Drinking Fluxx
text:
Scoring

End of the game
There is no points total. A player wins immediately on meeting the active Goal with their Keepers and any other stated conditions. If a Creeper prevents that win, it still prevents it even when the player has the listed Keepers. Simultaneous winners share the victory.

title: Drinking Fluxx
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Keeper: a persistent card in front of a player.
Goal: the current win condition.
New Rule: changes the rules in force.
Action: a one-off effect.
Creeper: a card with an ongoing drawback.
Surprise: a card playable at the timing stated on it.
Drink instruction: use the group’s agreed substitute when appropriate.

title: Moon
text:
Moon is a 2-5 player pick-and-pass base-building game played over three Eras. Build a Settlement that produces resources, establishes the five Flag types, and gains Hearts. Hearts earned during play, plus printed Hearts on grey Structures and Reputation cards at the end, determine the winner.



Every Era starts with Production, including the very first one, before any cards are drafted.
Every Construction turn requires exactly one Build or Assimilate action; the four extra actions are each limited to once that turn.
Hearts placed on Structures or Reputation cards score again in every later Era; do not remove them after scoring.

title: Moon
text:
Moon is a 2-5 player pick-and-pass base-building game played over three Eras. Build a Settlement that produces resources, establishes the five Flag types, and gains Hearts. Hearts earned during play, plus printed Hearts on grey Structures and Reputation cards at the end, determine the winner.



Every Era starts with Production, including the very first one, before any cards are drafted.
Every Construction turn requires exactly one Build or Assimilate action; the four extra actions are each limited to once that turn.
Hearts placed on Structures or Reputation cards score again in every later Era; do not remove them after scoring.

title: Moon
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Make a general supply of Hearts, Rovers, and Energy, Water, Biomass, and Metal. Put three Hearts below each Flag on the Flag Reward board and three Hearts on X. Reveal as many random Bronze, Silver, and Gold Reputation cards as there are players, except reveal three of each in a two-player game. Shuffle the three Structure decks and three Expedition decks separately; start a face-up Era I discard pile with one Structure card.

Table checklist

Give each player a Base, player aid, and two Rovers. A Base counts as both a blue and yellow Structure.
Give the First Expedition card to the starting player: use the 2-3 card for two or three players and the 4-5 card for four or five.
For two players, remove the Base, Expedition, and Era I/II Structure cards marked 3+ before setup. No Era III Structures are removed.
In Era I, deal Structure hands only after Production: eight cards at two players, seven at three or four, and six at five. In Eras II and III, first turn one Structure from that Era face up to begin a new discard pile.
Deal one current-Era Expedition card to every player except the holder of First Expedition; each hand therefore has Structure cards plus one Expedition card.

title: Moon
text:
Rounds and Phases
Each Era has Production, Construction, then Scoring. In Production, all players take everything shown by the white-arrow Production symbols in their Settlement. Blue Structures produce immediately when built as well as in later Production phases.

Construction turn

Starting with First Expedition, take turns clockwise. You must either Build one Structure from hand, paying its resource cost and already meeting all printed Flag requirements, or Assimilate one Structure by placing it on the discard pile and taking its trash-can reward.
Before or after that mandatory action, each of these optional actions may be used once: use the Expedition card’s bonus action, park one Rover, claim one Reputation card, and flip one pink Structure.
A Rover parks only on another player’s blue or yellow Structure. On blue, take its production immediately; on yellow, use its Flags for this turn’s Build requirement. The parking space remains blocked until Era end, when the Rover becomes that Structure owner’s Rover.
A Reputation card may be claimed only when its requirement is met; take its immediate or ongoing effect and keep it. Pink Structures are flipped for their once-per-Era effects.
After everyone has taken a turn, pass complete hands, including Expedition cards, left. Repeat until only Expedition cards remain. In a two-player game, the same player leads throughout Construction, then the other player leads next Era.
End Construction by passing First Expedition left, returning the other Expedition cards, taking parked Rovers into the owning players’ supplies, flipping pink cards back, and shuffling the discard pile back into the current Era deck.



Important exception
Flag requirements must already be in your Settlement, but a Rover parked on another player’s yellow Structure can supply Flags only for the Build made that turn. A Rover cannot park on your own cards, and one card has room for only one Rover (the Base has one blue and one yellow space).

title: Moon
text:
Scoring
Resolve each Flag reward in order. The player with the most of that Flag in their Settlement takes all Hearts below it. A tie goes to the tied player with more Rovers in their supply; if still tied, nobody takes the reward and the Hearts remain. Then each player gains Hearts equal to the Heart tokens on their Structures and Reputation cards, leaving those tokens in place.

End of an Era

Award all five Flag rewards, then score Heart tokens already placed on cards.
Remove one Heart from X, reducing the Excitement Value from 3 in Era I to 2 in Era II and 1 in Era III.
After Era I, put four Hearts below every Flag; after Era II, put five below every Flag. Unclaimed Hearts remain and add to the refill.
After Era III, do not refill. Add the Hearts already earned during the game to the printed Hearts on grey Structures and Reputation cards. Do not score Heart tokens on cards again.
The highest total wins. Ties go to the player with more Rovers, then fewer Reputation cards; a remaining tie is shared.

title: Moon
text:
Terminology

Settlement: Your Base, built Structures, and Hearts and Rovers on them; resources and Reputation cards are not part of it.
Build: Put a Structure into the appropriate Settlement area after paying costs and satisfying Flag requirements.
Assimilate: Discard a Structure from hand for its trash-can reward.
Rover: A token that can use another player’s blue production or yellow Flags for the turn.
Reputation card: A public, claimable card with a requirement, an effect, and printed endgame Hearts.

title: Chrononauts
text:
You are a time traveller changing history, collecting lost objects, and trying to reach the reality your Identity calls home.


You can win by restoring the reality on your Identity, putting the Artifacts named by your Mission on the table, or ending your turn with ten cards in hand. Watch all three routes because opponents can change the TimeLine under you.

title: Chrononauts
text:
You are a time traveller changing history, collecting lost objects, and trying to reach the reality your Identity calls home.


You can win by restoring the reality on your Identity, putting the Artifacts named by your Mission on the table, or ending your turn with ten cards in hand. Watch all three routes because opponents can change the TimeLine under you.

title: Chrononauts
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Build the table

Arrange the 32 double-sided TimeLine cards in the 8-by-4 Time Index grid, A1-8 through D1-8, with every card on its True History side: Ripplepoints blue and Linchpins purple.
Make separate shuffled piles for the other card types. Give each player one secret Identity, one secret Mission, and three cards from the main deck.
Everyone guesses the current time; the closest starts, then play proceeds clockwise.

Keep Identities and Missions secret until claiming victory. The TimeLine remains public and fixed in its indexed grid; its cards are flipped, not removed.

title: Chrononauts
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take a turn

Draw one card from the main deck.
Play one card from hand, or discard one if it cannot or should not be played. Resolve the card fully.
If the card was discarded instead of played, the player may discard a second card and draw one replacement: this is Killing Time.
Check only that active player’s victory conditions at the end of their turn. Shuffle the discard pile to form a draw deck only when a draw is required and the deck is empty.



Changing history

An Inverter flips a Linchpin, then all affected Ripplepoints are adjusted. Inverters never directly flip Ripplepoints.
A changed dependency creates a Paradox. A Patch may be played only on its matching Paradox, covering it; playing a Patch immediately draws one card.
Follow a Patch’s nullification icons whenever history changes. A nullified Patch is discarded; the underlying TimeLine card remains.
Artifacts and Gadgets stay face-up before their owner; Actions and Timewarps resolve then discard. A Memo From Your Future Self is the exception to turn ownership: it can cancel a card as it is played.

If 13 Paradoxes are visible at once, the game ends immediately and everybody loses. The 1962’ Patch creates the UberParadox: nothing after 1962 can be accessed, changed or collected from the future until it is cleared; later Paradoxes count as part of that one large Paradox. The 1945 Nexus can have three dependencies and four possible Patches, so check its playable and nullification icons especially carefully.

title: Chrononauts
text:
Scoring

End of the game
There is no points total. Claim victory only at the end of your own turn by meeting one condition:

Going Home: all three headlines on the Identity appear on the TimeLine; a Paradox blocks this route.
Mission: the three named Artifacts are face-up in front of the player, not merely in hand. Some Missions name any three from four.
Power and Success: the player has ten cards in hand, excluding Identity and Mission cards.

title: Chrononauts
text:
Terminology

Key terms

TimeLine: the shared chronological row of events.
Linchpin: a two-sided pivotal event, changed by an Inverter.
Ripplepoint: a dependent event that becomes a Paradox when its condition fails.
Patch: a card that covers its matching Paradox and grants an immediate draw.
Paradox: a contradiction created by the current TimeLine.
Artifact: a collectable object used by Missions.
Identity: your secret home-reality objective.
Mission: your secret list of three Artifacts.

Every card has a money value in the corner, but using a card as money is permanent: it stays in your bank and cannot later be used for its action or property side. Keep action cards in hand until their effect is useful.

title: Monopoly Deal
text:
Build a property portfolio while using money and action cards to charge rent, demand payment, and disrupt opponents.


Every card has a money value in the corner, but using a card as money is permanent: it stays in your bank and cannot later be used for its action or property side. Keep action cards in hand until their effect is useful.

title: Monopoly Deal
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Deal the game

Shuffle the full deck.
Deal five cards face-down to every player.
Put the remaining cards face-down as the draw pile.
Choose a first player; play proceeds clockwise.

Each player makes space for a bank and for property sets. Cards in hand stay secret; money and properties are face-up.

title: Monopoly Deal
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take a turn

Draw two cards. If you start the turn with no cards, draw five instead.
Play up to three cards total. You may play fewer or none.
Use each play as one of the following:

put a property or wild property in your collection;
put a money card, or an action card for its printed value, in your bank;
play an action card and resolve it.

Discard down to seven cards at the end of your turn.



Paying demands
When another player demands payment, pay only from face-up bank cards and properties. Choose what to give; you do not make change, and any overpayment stays with the recipient. You cannot pay with cards in hand. If you cannot pay the full amount, give everything you have in play.


Important action effects

Rent charges a player or all opponents as stated; add the rents of complete sets only when the card allows it.
Debt Collector and It’s My Birthday demand money, not a choice of cards from hand.
Sly Deal steals one property from an incomplete set; Forced Deal swaps properties between incomplete sets.
Deal Breaker steals a complete set. Just Say No cancels an action; another Just Say No can cancel that cancellation.

You may rearrange wild properties among your own sets during your turn, but not after another player has announced an action against them.

title: Monopoly Deal
text:
Scoring

End of the game
There is no points total. The first player with three complete property sets of different colours wins immediately, even if the final property was obtained by an action. Extra properties or houses/hotels are not needed for a set to count.

title: Monopoly Deal
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Bank: your pile of money cards and banked action cards.
Property set: properties of one colour collected together.
Complete set: the number of properties shown on the cards for that colour.
Wild property: a property card that can represent one of its printed colours.
Rent: a payment demanded by a rent action card.
Action card: a card with an immediate effect, such as charging rent or stealing property.

title: ROVE
text:
You are a damaged exploration robot, reconfiguring six modules to complete seven missions.



ROVE is a one-player spatial puzzle.
Complete seven missions to win; there is no points comparison.

title: ROVE
text:
You are a damaged exploration robot, reconfiguring six modules to complete seven missions.



ROVE is a one-player spatial puzzle.
Complete seven missions to win; there is no points comparison.

title: ROVE
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Shuffle the six Module cards and deal them active-side up in a two-row, three-column layout.
Shuffle the 12 double-sided Mission/Movement cards mission-side up. Reveal the top card above the modules as the first mission.
Draw five cards and turn them to their Movement side for your hand. For a harder game start with four; for Impossible, start with three. Your maximum hand size remains five.
Leave space for a discard pile.

title: ROVE
text:
Rounds and Phases

Solve the current mission

Earn movement points either by playing a Movement card from hand for the points at its top, or by matching its printed pattern before playing it to earn the points beneath that pattern.
Spend the points to move modules according to their arrows, resolving module abilities when useful.
After every move and ability, keep all modules unstacked, on an imaginary grid, and in one contiguous group. Corner contact counts as adjacent.
Complete the mission when the modules match its pattern. The named module must occupy its shown space; the other shown spaces can hold any modules. Patterns cannot be rotated or flipped, and may require only a subset of modules.
Cover the completed mission with the next mission card and draw one card if below five. Continue from the current layout.



Movement and abilities

The standard arrow moves its module any distance in a shown direction and may pass over modules. The short arrow moves it one space. The jumping arrow moves any distance in a shown direction but must pass over at least one module. The pushing arrow moves one space and pushes any module in its destination, and any chain beyond it, one space as well.
Each module ability is single-use: flip that module to its spent side before resolving it. Brain repositions another module adjacent to Brain; Coil repositions itself to any valid location; Gripper activates an adjacent module’s ability; Laser swaps two modules; Motor shifts any module one space in any direction; Sensor draws a card if below five.
A Movement card stays current while it has points. Discard it, losing unspent points, when its last point is spent, when another Movement card is played, or when a mission is completed.



Deck pressure
When the deck is empty, turn the discard pile mission-side up to form a new deck without shuffling it. If you cannot complete the current mission, you lose.

title: ROVE
text:
Scoring
ROVE has no score or tiebreak. Complete seven missions to win; fail to complete the current mission to lose.

title: ROVE
text:
Terminology

Module: one of the six robot cards.
Mission: the current target pattern.
Movement point: a point earned from the current Movement card and spent to move a module.
Adjacent: modules touching edge-to-edge or corner-to-corner.
Spent: a module whose one-use ability has been used.

title: Fluxx Remixx
text:
Fluxx Remixx is a more chaotic version of Fluxx, with music-themed cards, changing rules, and Goals that decide which Keepers win.


The basic Fluxx structure remains, but Remixx adds Surprises that interrupt play at their stated timing. A new Goal, Rule, or Surprise can overturn a good plan immediately.

title: Fluxx Remixx
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Deal the game

Shuffle the deck and deal three cards to every player.
Put the remaining cards face-down as the draw pile and leave room for discards.
Choose a first player.
Start with no cards in play and the Basic Rule Draw 1, Play 1.

If the draw pile is exhausted, shuffle the discard pile into a replacement draw pile. Cards in front of players stay in play.

title: Fluxx Remixx
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take a turn

Draw the required number of cards.
Play the required number, resolving each card immediately.
Enforce active Hand and Keeper Limits after playing.
Check the active Goal before the next player begins.



Cards and interruptions

Keepers remain in front of their owner.
Goals and New Rules replace the existing card of the same type.
Actions resolve once and are discarded.
A Surprise is playable only at the timing printed on it. Resolve it before returning to the interrupted effect or turn.

If a new Draw or Play rule appears during your turn, use it immediately when it can still affect that turn. If an instruction cannot be completed, do as much as possible. Latest card text beats a conflicting general rule.

title: Fluxx Remixx
text:
Scoring

End of the game
There is no score. The first time one or more players satisfy the active Goal with their Keepers, those players win immediately. This can happen on any player’s turn, including while resolving an Action or Surprise.

title: Fluxx Remixx
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Keeper: a persistent card in front of a player.
Goal: the current win condition.
New Rule: changes the rules in force.

title: Radlands
text:
Radlands is a two-player duel. Each player protects three camps, recruits people and schedules events, spending a short-lived supply of water to destroy the opponent’s camps first.


People occupy columns in front of camps and can protect cards behind them. Events enter a three-space queue and count down to resolution. Cards in hand can instead be discarded for their printed junk effect, so every draw is a choice between an immediate effect and a future play.

title: Radlands
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Build each tribe

Shuffle the camp deck, then each player draws six camps and secretly chooses three. Put the three chosen camps face down in a row, leaving room for two people in front of each; reveal them together. Return the unchosen camps and camp deck to the box.
Each player takes a Water Silo, a Raiders card, a player aid, and three white water discs. Shuffle the shared draw deck, make space for its discard pile, and put black extra-water discs in a central supply.
Each player draws a starting hand equal to the sum of the black-box values on their three camps. Flip a water disc to choose the start player.

For a recommended first game, the experienced player uses Arcade, Victory Totem, and Mercenary Camp; the other uses Garage, Railgun, and Supply Depot.

title: Radlands
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take a turn
Starting with the start player, take turns until the game ends. Complete these phases in order:

Events: if an event occupies the front space of your queue, resolve it and discard it. Then advance every event in your queue one space towards the front.
Replenish: draw one card, then collect three white water discs. The start player collects only one water on their first turn. Water never carries between turns.
Actions: take any number of actions, in any order. When finished, return all white and black water discs to their supplies.



Spend water on actions
You may repeat these actions while you can pay their costs:

Play a person: pay its cost and place it in front of any camp, even a destroyed camp. A column holds at most two people; place the new person in front of or behind an existing one. If every column is full, first destroy one of your people to make room. A newly played person is not ready.
Play an event: pay its cost and place it in its numbered queue space; if occupied, use the first available space behind it. If none is available, it cannot be played. A zero-time event resolves immediately, then is discarded with its payment.
Draw a card: spend two water to draw one card.
Junk a card: discard a hand card to resolve the junk icon at its top left.
Take Water Silo: spend one water to take it into hand. Junking it grants extra water, then returns it to your play area instead of the discard pile.
Use an ability: pay the printed cost on one ready camp or person, resolve all its text and icons, then mark it not ready.



Damage, readiness, and Raiders
Damage turns a person or camp sideways; damage it again to destroy it. A damaged person is not ready, while a damaged camp may still be ready. Unless an effect says otherwise, damage, injure, and destroy target an opponent’s unprotected card: a card with no card in front of it. Destroyed people are discarded, and destroyed camps are flipped. A punk is a face-down person with no abilities; it is destroyed by damage and returns face down to the top of the draw deck.
Camps are ready unless their ability was used this turn. A person is not ready if it entered play, was restored, used an ability, or is damaged this turn. Water on a card also marks it not ready; use a black disc to mark a zero-cost card or ability not ready.
When an effect raids, put Raiders into the third queue space if absent; otherwise advance it one space if the space ahead is empty, resolving it if it is already at the front. When Raiders resolves, the opponent chooses one camp to damage, even if protected, then returns Raiders to its owner.

title: Radlands
text:
Scoring

Win, draw, or lose
There are no victory points. You win immediately when all three opponent camps are destroyed. If the draw deck empties, shuffle the discard pile to make a new deck. If it empties a second time, the game is a draw.

title: Radlands
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Camp: one of the three objectives a player protects.
Column: a camp and up to two people in front of it.
Person: a persistent, white-bordered card in a column.
Event: a card that waits in an event queue unless it has zero time.
Ready: able to use an ability.
Water: the resource spent during one turn; unspent water is returned at cleanup.
Junk: discard a hand card for its printed instant effect.
Unprotected: a camp or person with no card in front of it.

title: Wyrmspan
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Build the shared display

Choose one Dragon Guild and use the correct player-count side.
Reveal the round-end objective tiles and prepare the cave-card and dragon-card displays.
Each player takes a mat, adventurer, Guild marker, starting egg, and starting cards.



Choose a start

Your mat starts with the leftmost space of each cave excavated.
Choose four cards from three dragon cards and three cave cards.
Choose any three food resources. Keep your choices hidden until play begins.

title: Wyrmspan
text:
Rounds and Phases

Start of a round

The game has exactly four rounds.
At the start of every round, gain 6 coins and 1 egg.
Coins may be saved from an earlier round, subject to the end-of-turn limit.



Take turns
On a turn, spend coins to take one action. The main actions are:

Excavate: play a cave card into an available cave space, pay its placement cost if any, and take its when-played benefit.
Entice: play a dragon into an excavated, unoccupied space, paying the resources and any egg shown on that dragon.
Explore: send your adventurer through one cave from left to right. Resolve each dragon encountered in order and take the benefit at the cave’s end if reached.
Advance on the Dragon Guild: pay the listed cost to claim an available Guild benefit and move your marker.



Passing and cleanup

When you cannot or do not wish to take another action, pass for the round.
Once everyone has passed, resolve the round-end goal, then refresh the shared cave and dragon displays for the next round.
At the end of each of your turns, discard down to at most 9 cards, 9 coins, and 9 resource tokens.



Important exceptions

Most card abilities are optional. An ability that offers something to other players must activate, but each player chooses whether to take the benefit.
A dragon that says “in this cave” means its own row, not all three caves.
Reaching a stop sign or the end of an explored cave sends the adventurer back to Base Camp and ends that turn.
You may exchange two resources for one resource of your choice at any time.

Excavate: add a cave card and make a space available for a dragon.
Entice: play a dragon into an excavated space.
Explore: move the adventurer through one cave, activating dragons in order.
Hatchling: a baby dragon with an egg cost, a feeding effect, and a later growth effect.
Tuck / cache: store a card beneath a dragon or a resource on it.
Dragon Guild: a shared progression board with limited benefits and end-game scoring.

title: Micro Architects
text:
In this 2-4 player city-building game, make the highest-scoring city over three rounds. You place Buildings into the eight four-space blocks of your personal City board, then score the two current Goals, your Landmarks, and your Services each round.



Take from the current topmost non-empty Building row: everyone gets one Building on every turn.

title: Micro Architects
text:
In this 2-4 player city-building game, make the highest-scoring city over three rounds. You place Buildings into the eight four-space blocks of your personal City board, then score the two current Goals, your Landmarks, and your Services each round.



Take from the current topmost non-empty Building row: everyone gets one Building on every turn.

Landmarks need a Requirement tile. Its placement preference and neighbouring-Building preference determine its score every round.

title: Micro Architects
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Place the Architects board centrally. Shuffle the Goal cards and lay out three pairs above it; only these six Goals are used. Shuffle the Service deck, reveal three cards, put all Buildings in the bag, and make the round-one Building rows: two rows of 10 for two players, three rows of 9 for three, or four rows of 8 for four. Draw six Buildings for Backup Plans.

Table checklist

Shuffle the Requirement tiles. Reveal one for every Landmark in the first Building row and Backup Plans combined; leave the rest facedown as a stack.
Give each player a City board, scoring token, and six Action tokens. Put two tokens in their play area and four aside for later rounds.
Put Boats within reach. Give the First Player card to whoever most recently held a hammer.
Each City block has four spaces: two by the river and two by the mountains, and is either green or grey. Buildings may go in any free space.
When taking a Landmark, choose an available Requirement tile and put it beside that Landmark’s block. A block can hold at most four Buildings, irrespective of type.

title: Micro Architects
text:
Rounds and Phases
Play three rounds, each with an Action, Scoring, and Cleanup phase. Beginning with the first player and proceeding clockwise, a player must take one Building from the current topmost non-empty row and place it. When that row empties, reveal Requirement tiles for the Landmarks in the next row and Backup Plans, pass first player left, and continue with that new first player. Scoring begins once the final row is empty.

Action phase order

On a turn, take and place one Building from the current row. Filling the final space of a block gives you one Boat; put it by that block.
Before or after taking that Building, spend up to two Action tokens, one per action. Overhaul swaps two City Buildings; if a Landmark moves, move one Requirement tile from its old block to its new block.
Backup Plan swaps one City Building with a displayed Backup Plan Building. Take a Requirement tile if the incoming Building is a Landmark; return one from its block if the outgoing Building is a Landmark.
Relocation moves one Building to a free City space. If this newly fills a block without a Boat, gain that Boat.
Demanding Residents reveals two extra Services. You may then spend two Boats for one of the five; discard or refill the other extra cards as directed by which card you take.
At any time on your turn, spend two Boats for one available Service, immediately refilling the three-card offer. You cannot own duplicate Services. Alternatively, spend one Boat to recover two used Action tokens; both Boat options may be used any number of times.



Cleanup
After rounds one and two, turn the scored Goals facedown, return all Backup Plan Buildings to the bag and draw six replacements, then create the next round’s Building rows. Round two uses 2x8, 3x9, or 4x12 Buildings; round three uses 2x10, 3x9, or 4x8. Discard leftover Requirement tiles, reveal replacements for Landmarks in the new first row and Backup Plans, give every player two Action tokens, and pass first player left. Skip Cleanup after round three.

title: Micro Architects
text:
Scoring
Score at the end of every round, in the same order. Goals award their printed points for every qualifying block or set of blocks. Each Landmark Requirement scores separately: one point for its Landmark’s correct block/location preference, plus up to three points for Buildings of either indicated type in that Landmark’s block. A Landmark can score only its own Requirement tile. Each Service scores two points per indicated pair of Building types anywhere in your city; the same Building can contribute to several Services.

Scoring order

Score both face-up Goals for the round.
Score every Landmark Requirement tile.
Score every Service.
After round three, add two points per unused Boat and one point per unused Action token.
The highest total wins. On a tie, the player with fewer Landmarks wins; any remaining tie is shared.

title: Micro Architects
text:
Terminology

Building Plans: The rows of Buildings from which players must currently choose.
Landmark: A black Building that receives a Requirement tile when taken.
Backup Plans: The six-Building alternative display used by the Backup Plan action.
Boat: A token earned for completing blocks and spent on Services or recovering Action tokens.
Service: A scoring card bought with two Boats.

title: Dobble

The matching symbol may differ in size, position, or orientation. A player must name the shared picture to claim or move a card.

title: Dobble
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Shuffle the 55-card deck and choose one of the five games below before dealing. All players search simultaneously; there are no turns.

Towering Inferno
Deal each player one face-down card. Make a face-up centre draw pile from the rest. Everyone reveals their card; the first player to name its match with the centre card takes that centre card onto their own face-up pile. The newly exposed centre card starts the next search.


The Well
Set one card aside face down. Deal the remaining cards equally into face-down personal draw piles, then turn the set-aside card, or an undealt extra, face up in the centre. Everyone reveals the top card of their own pile.

title: Dobble
text:
Rounds and Phases

Play The Well

Compare your top personal card with the centre card.
First to name their shared symbol places their personal card on the centre card and reveals their next personal card.
Continue until a player exhausts their personal draw pile; that player wins.



The other games

Towering Inferno: continue claiming centre cards until its draw pile is empty. The player with the most claimed cards wins.
Hot Potato: give every player one face-down card to hold, then reveal together. Name a match with another player’s card and put every card in your hand into that player’s hand. Continue until one player holds all cards; put them before that player and deal another round. After the agreed fixed number of rounds, at least five, the player with the most cards loses.
Catch Them All!: put one card face up in the centre and deal one face-down card to each player. Reveal together, then name a match between the centre card and any revealed card to claim that revealed card face down. When all are claimed, put the centre card on the bottom of the draw pile and deal again. When the draw pile is exhausted, most claimed cards wins.
The Poisoned Gift: deal one face-down card to each player and make a face-up centre draw pile from the rest. Reveal personal cards together. Name a match between the centre card and another player’s card to put the centre card on that player’s pile; the next exposed centre card continues play. When the draw pile is empty, fewest cards wins.



Quick teaching tip
Choose a symbol on one card and scan the other for it; never expect a match to occupy the same place or size.

title: Dobble
text:
Scoring
Each mini-game’s end condition and winner are given above. The supplied rules do not specify a separate tiebreak; a tied result remains a tie unless players agree otherwise before play.

title: Dobble
text:
Terminology

Symbol: a picture on a card.
Match: the one symbol shared by two cards.
Centre card: the face-up card used for the current comparison.
Mini-game: one of Dobble’s five setups and victory conditions.

title: Kelp: Shark vs Octopus
text:
This asymmetric duel takes place in a kelp forest. The Octopus hides, moves blocks and develops its deck; the Shark patrols with dice, searches blocks and tries to strike the Octopus.



Kelp is strictly a two-player game.
One player is the Octopus; one is the Shark. The Octopus takes the first turn.
The Octopus wins by placing all four food blocks on the Food Track, or when the Shark places a seventh die on the Hunger Track. The Shark wins only by striking the Octopus with a red die and matching its confrontation choice.

title: Kelp: Shark vs Octopus
text:
This asymmetric duel takes place in a kelp forest. The Octopus hides, moves blocks and develops its deck; the Shark patrols with dice, searches blocks and tries to strike the Octopus.



Kelp is strictly a two-player game.
One player is the Octopus; one is the Shark. The Octopus takes the first turn.
The Octopus wins by placing all four food blocks on the Food Track, or when the Shark places a seventh die on the Hunger Track. The Shark wins only by striking the Octopus with a red die and matching its confrontation choice.

title: Kelp: Shark vs Octopus
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Seat the players on their named sides. Put 7 blue Current dice, 3 yellow Search dice and 1 red Strike die in the Shark bag; make four face-up Shark cards, the deck, and four unflipped Growth tiles. Put both sets of three confrontation cards face-down beside the board.
Separate the non-starter Octopus cards into face-up Move, Hide, Learn and Eat piles. Put the matching food block on the top Eat card; put the other food, three named traps, a shell and a double shell beside the piles.
Put the Octopus, one trap and seven shells in the Octopus bag. The Octopus secretly draws and places all nine blocks upright in the board spaces, then puts the bag aside. Hidden blocks show their icons only to the Octopus.
Set aside Fast Learning. Shuffle the remaining starter cards as the Octopus draw pile; take Fast Learning plus three cards, set hand size to four, and have the Octopus place the Shark on any den Current space facing the centre.

title: Kelp: Shark vs Octopus
text:
Rounds and Phases

Alternating turns
Players alternate whole turns, beginning with the Octopus, until an immediate win condition is met.


The Octopus turn
Take exactly two actions; the same action may be chosen twice.

Play a card: reveal the stated number of hidden blocks as its cost (the double shell counts as two), complete its effect, and put it in an action slot. A card cannot be played unless its full effect can happen.
Draw: if below hand size, draw up to it; an empty hand must use this action. Shuffle the discard pile only when a draw is required and the draw pile is empty.
Discard and hide: discard one card, then hide one revealed block if possible.

At turn end, discard played cards. Move swaps orthogonally adjacent blocks without changing their hidden/revealed state; a shuffle returns chosen hidden blocks to the bag and the Shark chooses their replacement empty spaces. Learn gains the stated mix of top cards and blocks: gained cards usually go to discard, while each gained block replaces a revealed board block and enters revealed. An Eat card comes with its matching food block as one Learn gain.
To eat, the Octopus and matching food must be orthogonally adjacent, then play the matching Eat card as an action, reveal both blocks, replace the food with a revealed spare shell, put the food on the next Food Track space, and trash the Eat card. Its one-time food effect may be used before, between or after actions.


The Shark turn
Perform these steps in order; only Draw & Roll and Move are compulsory.

Draw & Roll: draw and roll two dice (plus unlocked bonuses). Blue dice may be placed on any empty Current space.
Move: move forward to an empty Current space. The Shark cannot stand still, reverse, or move backwards; it may choose a direction when starting at a den. It may skip a Current or a connected chain whose values strictly decrease, moving only the first skipped Current to Growth.
Search/Strike: use yellow and/or red dice on up to two orthogonally adjacent zones, each die at least the zone value and with only one die per space. Search reveals a hidden block; Strike reveals a block and attacks it. Used yellow dice go to Growth; a red die goes to Hunger after a miss, trap, or escaped confrontation. Unused dice remain for Energy.
Growth: place used yellow dice and the first Current used from left to right. When a tile receives its third die, return those dice to the bag and flip it for its permanent ability. Red dice never go here.
Energy: place all remaining pool dice in stored Energy. With one or two dice the Shark may buy; with three it must buy if able. Buy any number of face-up cards up to the total pips, add their dice to the bag immediately, refill the display, and return unspent dice to the bag. Spending Energy moves exactly one stored die to Hunger; if no displayed card is affordable, return all dice without Hunger.



Attacking

A red Strike die that reveals the Octopus starts a confrontation.
Both players secretly choose one remaining coloured confrontation card and reveal together.
If colours match, the Shark wins immediately. Otherwise the Octopus performs its escape effect, then trashes its used card and the Shark card of that matching colour.
Thus the second confrontation is a 50/50 choice; by the third the remaining colours must match.



Important exceptions

A Search can reveal the Octopus but does not attack it; shells and food have no search effect, while traps trigger on Search or Strike.
If the Shark’s bag is empty when dice are needed, remove Current dice from the board until two dice can be drawn. If a second chosen Search/Strike zone ceases to be adjacent after the first reveal, return its die to the bag.
The seventh Hunger die ends the game immediately in the Octopus’s favour. This includes a die moved there after a Strike or spent Energy.

title: Kelp: Shark vs Octopus
text:
Scoring
There is no points total. The Octopus wins immediately by eating its fourth food block or exhausting the Shark with the seventh Hunger die. The Shark wins immediately on the first confrontation in which its colour matches the Octopus’s choice.

title: Kelp: Shark vs Octopus
text:
Terminology

Energy: unspent rolled dice whose pips buy Shark cards.
Learn: an Octopus card that gains a new option and its matching food block.
Eat: the matching card/food pairing acquired through Learn.
Confrontation cards: simultaneous coloured choices; matching colours win the attack.
Hunger Track: permanent dice from Strikes and Energy spending; seven exhaust the Shark.

text:
Cytress is a 1-5 player engine-builder. In the standard 2-5 player game, build faction lifepaths, deploy crews onto the Cytress mini-map, then ascend them through waste tubes to the three levels of Stratos. When the tube supply runs out, score Prestige for crews, majorities, controlled tubes, and bounties.



Corpocrat lifepaths provide Phase 1 income, Privateer lifepaths reward rivals’ scouting, Rover lifepaths improve trade ratios, and Hooligang lifepaths discount matching costs.

title: Cytress
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Use one random mini-map tile per player, the matching 1-3 or 4+ player sides of the faction boards, and the relevant bounty cards. Construct Stratos, randomise the Cytress board side, reveal three cards from each faction deck and five Stratolites, and place seven tube sections per player near Stratos. The remaining tubes stay out of reach until game end is triggered.

Setup discipline

Each player chooses a side of a randomly dealt rebel board and receives its leader, three transports, twelve crews, and a resource tracker.
Start every resource at 2, with a maximum of 25. The resources are Creds, Tech, Glow, and Ammo.
The most recent cyberpunk-film viewer takes the first-player marker.
In a 2-player game, only the designated 3-resource scout spot is available in each district. In 2-3 players, every player scouts twice each round; in 4-5 players, each scouts once.

title: Cytress
text:
Rounds and Phases
Play repeated rounds of four phases. Phase 3 has a normal Travel stage followed by Extra Travel for transports that visited Stratos. Players can still gain intel cards after their crews are gone, but a tube can only be placed on a hex containing their own crew.

How to teach a turn

Income, simultaneously: gain every resource icon in your Corpocrat lifepath.
Scout Districts: in first-player order, put your leader on an empty scout spot of a faction and gain its printed resource plus one matching resource for each of your crews already on Stratos. Every other player gains matching resources shown in their Privateer lifepath; the active scout does not. In 2-3 players, repeat the process with a different faction.
Travel: players alternate moving one of their three transports to a landing pad until all have moved. Meeting a faction pays its cost, takes and refills one intel card, adds it to the matching lifepath, places a crew on an empty matching-colour mini-map hex, and may spy on one adjacent rival for resources matching all hex colours occupied by that rival’s adjacent crews.
Other Travel actions are: Stratolite or Renegade to pay for a 1-, 2-, or 3-high tube (cost 5, 11, or 18) and ascend that crew to the matching Stratos level; Enforcer for a bounty and one optional immediate benefit; Fixer for free intel without crew placement, one reserved Stratolite, and next phase’s first-player marker; or Merchant for up to two directed trades. A Stratolite requires its shown resource and hex type; Renegade accepts any one resource type and any hex with your crew. Hooligang discounts apply to the matching resource cost.
Extra Travel: in turn order, each transport left on Stratos after meeting a Stratolite takes one more Travel action, but must leave Stratos and cannot meet another Stratolite. Reset: discard the rightmost Stratolite, shift the rest right, refill the leftmost slot, and return leaders and transports.



Version warning
The game enters its final round when the allocated tube sections are exhausted in Travel or Extra Travel. Use extra tubes from the box to finish that round, then score rather than resetting.

title: Cytress
text:
Scoring
Add Prestige for each crew on Stratos: 5 on level 1, 10 on level 2, and 15 on level 3. On each level, every player tied for the most crews also earns its majority award: level 1 is 3 per crew on all of Stratos, level 2 is 3 per card in the longest lifepath, and level 3 is 6 per complete set of the four faction target icons across lifepaths. Control each tube with a strict majority of crews on its adjacent mini-map hexes; tied tubes score nobody. Controlled tubes score 3, 5, or 7 for heights 1, 2, or 3. Finally score bounties for matching target icons: 2 Prestige each in 2-3 players; in 4-5 players use each bounty’s printed 1- or 2-Prestige rate. Highest total wins; ties share victory.

title: Cytress
text:
Terminology

Lifepath: One of four engine rows receiving faction intel cards.
Crew: A token placed on the mini-map or ascended to Stratos.
Waste tube: A 1-3 section route that moves one crew to its matching Stratos level.
Stratolite: A card that fixes the resource and mini-map hex type for a tube drop.
Bounty: A faction-target scoring card taken from the Enforcers.

title: Hideous Abominations
text:
Setting up

Place the Grand Prizes face up between all players.
Place the Score cards deck next to the Grand Prizes, leaving a space below to place them as awards. Set aside the tie-breaker prizes.
Shuffle the Body Part deck and place the top 3 Body Part cards in the middle between players - this is the Buffet. Place the remaining Body Part deck next to the Buffet.
Provide each player with a Torso card (all Torsos are functionally the same).
Deal 3 Body Part cards to each player.
Place the Bolt tokens within reach of players.

title: Hideous Abominations
text:
Rounds
Players take turns. Each turn, players take the following actions:

Roll the die:

Draw: Draw 2 tiles and place them in your hand from either the Buffet piles or from the top of the deck.
Dig: Pick up one of the piles from the Buffet, dig through it and select any 2 tiles. Return the pile in any order. If a pile only contains 1 tile, draw your second tile blind from the Body Parts deck.

title: Innovation
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Prepare the ages

Separate and shuffle cards into the ten age supply piles. Without looking, set aside one card from each age 1-9 as the nine normal Achievements; place the five Special Achievements nearby.
Each player draws two age-1 cards, simultaneously melds one as their first board card, and keeps the other in hand.
The player whose melded card title is closest to A alphabetically goes first. In a four-player game, the first two players take only one action on their first turns; otherwise, every turn has two actions.

title: Innovation
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take two actions
On your turn take exactly two actions, in any order, and you may repeat one. Choose from:

Draw: draw into hand from the pile matching the highest-value top card on your board. If that pile is empty, use the next higher non-empty pile.
Meld: place a hand card on top of the matching-colour stack, continuing its current splay if any.
Dogma: activate one top card and resolve all its effects in order.
Achieve: claim an available normal Achievement if your score is at least five times its age and you have a top card of at least that value. Score is a threshold, not a cost.



Resolve dogma carefully
At the start of a Dogma action, count the featured icon on every player’s board; do not recount during the action. For each non-demand effect, eligible opponents with at least as many of that icon perform it clockwise before the active player. For each “I Demand” effect, opponents with fewer icons perform it clockwise; those with at least as many are immune.
Complete one effect before the next and do as much as possible. If any opponent’s shared effect changed the game, the active player takes one free Draw action after the whole Dogma action. Effects marked for yourself only are not shared.


Splaying and card procedures
Splay a colour left, right, or up to expose respectively one, two, or three icons from each covered card. Unsplay before changing direction. A stack of zero or one card is unsplayed. To tuck, place a card at the bottom of its colour stack; to score, place it face down in the score pile; to return, place it face down at the bottom of its supply pile.
If a draw needs an empty age, draw from the next higher available age. If a draw requires an age higher than 10, the game ends immediately. An effect that says a player wins does so immediately; one requiring a single player with the most of something fails entirely on a tie.

title: Innovation
text:
Scoring

Achievements and endgame
Each scored card is worth its age in points. Claiming a normal Achievement does not spend those points. Claim Special Achievements immediately when their printed condition is met; if players become eligible simultaneously, resolve the tie in clockwise turn order from the current player.
Win immediately with six achievements in a two-player game, five with three players, or four with four players; normal and special achievements both count. If nobody has won when a card above age 10 must be drawn, highest score wins; then most achievements; a remaining tie is a draw.

title: Innovation
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Board: all cards a player has in play.
Top card: the completely visible card of a colour stack.
Meld: play a hand card onto its colour stack.
Dogma: activate a top card’s effects.
Share: an eligible opponent performs a non-demand effect before the active player.
Demand: an effect performed by opponents with fewer featured icons.
Splay: offset a stack to expose icons on cards beneath.
Score pile: face-down scored cards, whose total age is your score.

title: My City
text:
Build a city from its first settlement to industrialisation. My City is a 2-4 player legacy game of 24 episodes: your board is permanently altered as the campaign develops. Three episodes make a chapter, and each chapter introduces rules and components through a sealed envelope. The same group is best, but a new player may take over a departed player’s city.



In the legacy campaign, each player keeps one animal board for all 24 episodes. At the end of every episode, remove the buildings, reset the score marker to 10, then make only the permanent changes the current chapter instructs.
Do not open a later envelope. Each episode can be played separately, but the three episodes in a chapter are designed to be played together.
The reverse side offers the repeatable Eternity mode. It is a later-game configuration; at least one player should already know episodes 1-5. It uses identical boards and is suitable for players who have not played the campaign.
