title: My City
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Legacy play

Give each player their animal-side board, matching 24 buildings, and a score marker on 10. Put buildings face-up beside their owner. The three building colours are residential (yellow), administrative (red), and industrial (blue).
Shuffle the 24 Construction cards into a face-down deck. Open only the envelope for the current chapter; read its rules and keep its scoring/allocation sheet visible.
Apply all current episode instructions, including any stickers or extra components. Unless told otherwise, stickers go on empty, undecorated meadow squares with a small central square, after all buildings have been removed.



Repeatable play

Use the reverse side of each board, with score markers on 10. Each player takes 27 buildings: eight of each colour plus three churches. Ignore campaign stickers and extra campaign buildings.
Shuffle the 24 basic Construction cards, the three church cards, and the Prohibition card: 28 cards in all. Do not add campaign-only cards.
The Eternity board also includes wells and two gold deposits. These, churches, and the Prohibition card are specific to this mode.

title: My City
text:
Rounds and Phases

A building step

Reveal the next Construction card. All active players take the pictured building and place it immediately and simultaneously; there is no holding a piece for a later turn.
A building may cover empty meadow, rocks, trees, and (in Eternity mode) wells or gold deposits. It may not cover mountain or forest, overlap another building, or straddle the river. It may cover part of the river while remaining entirely on one bank.
Your first building must run along the river, not merely touch it at a corner. Every later building must share at least one edge with an existing building. Corner contact is not adjacency; buildings on opposite banks do count as adjacent if their edges meet across the river.
Once placed, a building never moves. If you cannot or do not wish to place the revealed building, either pass or leave the episode/game. Passing turns that building face-down and costs 1 point, but you remain active. Leaving turns it face-down at no cost and means you place no more buildings.



Important exceptions

You cannot pass while your score marker is at 0. If you cannot or will not build then, you must leave the episode/game.
In Eternity mode, churches must be built. If you cannot build a revealed church, you must leave rather than pass.
When Prohibition appears in Eternity mode, immediately reveal one further card. Its building is forbidden: nobody builds it, everyone turns that piece face-down, and play continues with the following card. This also applies if the forbidden piece is a church.
In Eternity mode, the first player to cover both gold deposits announces it and gains 3 points immediately; all players who achieve this in the same turn gain the 3 points.



End of an episode
The episode or Eternity game ends when every player has left it or all Construction cards have been revealed. In the campaign, score the episode, award progress circles and the instructed stickers, then clear buildings and reset score markers before the next episode.

title: My City
text:
Scoring

Legacy episode scoring
Start from the score marker, including any points gained or lost during the episode, then score the current episode sheet in its stated order. The base scoring is +1 per visible tree, -1 per visible rock, and -1 per empty meadow square. A square with two trees or rocks is worth two points; later single-tree squares are worth one. A player reaching 50 immediately checks one progress circle, stops scoring, and remains on 50; negative points below 0 are remembered and offset later positive points in that episode.
For the episode ranking, at 3-4 players first place checks two progress circles and second place checks one. At 2 players, only first place checks two. Break a tied score by comparing the number of empty meadow squares in the top row, then each lower row until one player has fewer. Check progress circles from left to right, top row first. After episode 24, the player with the most progress circles wins the campaign.


Eternity scoring
Score in this order:

Each visible double-tree meadow square: +2.
Each visible double-rock meadow square: -2.
For each building colour, score the size of its largest edge-adjacent group.
Each church with at least one adjacent building of each of the three colours: +3. Churches are not a colour.
Each well with a building on all four sides: +4.
Each empty meadow square: -1.

The highest total wins. Resolve a tie by the same row-by-row fewest-empty-meadows comparison used in the campaign.

title: My City
text:
Terminology

Episode: One game in the 24-part legacy campaign; three episodes form a chapter.
Construction card: The shared card that tells every active player which building to place.
Adjacent: Sharing an edge, including across the river; corner contact does not count.
Progress circle: A permanent campaign award. The most after episode 24 wins.
Leave: Stop placing buildings for the current episode/game without losing a point for the revealed building.
Pass: Decline one revealed building, lose 1 point, and remain active.

title: Tussie Mussie
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Shuffle all 18 Flower cards into a face-down deck and leave room for a discard pile.
The player who most recently smelled a flower is the first player.
Play three rounds. Each player will collect four cards per round.

title: Tussie Mussie
text:
Rounds and Phases

Make an offer

The active offerer draws two cards, looks at them, and places one face up and one face down as an offer to the recipient. The recipient may not inspect the face-down card.
The recipient chooses one card and adds it as the rightmost card in their arrangement, preserving its orientation.
The offerer adds the other card as the rightmost card in their own arrangement, also preserving its orientation.



Complete the round

With two players, alternate making offers until both arrangements contain four cards.
With three or four players, the first player offers left and offers continue clockwise until everyone has two cards. The first player then offers right and offers continue counterclockwise until everyone has four.
At round end, move each player’s Keepsakes toward them into a second row in their original columns, then reveal them face up. Cards remain adjacent to the cards immediately left and right, whether in Bouquet or Keepsakes.
Players simultaneously resolve any card effects labelled “Before Scoring,” in any order each player chooses.

title: Tussie Mussie
text:
Scoring

Score each arrangement from left to right after Before Scoring actions. Every heart icon is worth one point, plus each flower’s own scoring condition.
Record the round scores. If fewer than three rounds have been completed, shuffle all 18 cards together and begin again; the first player rotates clockwise.
After round three, the highest combined total wins.


Tie handling
Tied players compare the flowers in their final-round arrangements. The player with the first flower name alphabetically wins the tie.

title: Tussie Mussie
text:
Terminology

Offer: two cards, one face up and one face down, presented to a recipient.
Arrangement: the left-to-right cards a player has collected this round.
Bouquet: the face-up cards in an arrangement.
Keepsakes: the face-down cards in an arrangement.

title: Stellar Expedition
text:
In this 2-4 player exploration game, take a faction through a Space Gate and earn Expedition points across eight rounds. Discover locations, recruit a crew by building Embassies, meet Expedition requirements, and make the most of limited movement and resources before the Gate closes.



The first three rounds are Exploration rounds: the first Embassy on a new Location is discounted by 3, then 2, then 1 Raw Material.
Crew used for an Expedition or Encounter go to Transit and cannot be used again that round.
Three Embassies at one Recruiting Location double its production from the following round and immediately award one Expedition point.

title: Stellar Expedition
text:
In this 2-4 player exploration game, take a faction through a Space Gate and earn Expedition points across eight rounds. Discover locations, recruit a crew by building Embassies, meet Expedition requirements, and make the most of limited movement and resources before the Gate closes.



The first three rounds are Exploration rounds: the first Embassy on a new Location is discounted by 3, then 2, then 1 Raw Material.
Crew used for an Expedition or Encounter go to Transit and cannot be used again that round.
Three Embassies at one Recruiting Location double its production from the following round and immediately award one Expedition point.

title: Stellar Expedition
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Put the Space Gate in the middle. Each player chooses a faction, takes its Dashboard, 12 Embassy cubes and Location card, then places its matching Starting Location adjacent to the Gate. Put a Spaceship and one Embassy on that Starting Location; take its Captain and level-one Crew card, leaving the level-two and level-three cards on the table. Every player starts with five Raw Materials, two Crystals, and one Influence.

Table checklist

Combine the corresponding face-up Location and Crew decks, shuffle the remaining Location tiles, and place the Gate token on round 1.
Shuffle the Bronze, Silver, and Gold Expedition decks. Draft starting Expeditions by taking two cards of each type, choosing and passing until each player has one Expedition of each type; reshuffle the rest into their decks.
Shuffle Encounter, Upgrade, and Damage decks. Reveal six Upgrades as the store.
Choose a first player and give them the First Player token. The player to their left will become first player after every round.
Starting Locations are Recruiting Locations with one prebuilt Embassy. Recruiting Locations can produce resources and support Embassies; Anomalies cannot support either.

title: Stellar Expedition
text:
Rounds and Phases
Play eight rounds. Work through all four phases in order, with the first player and then clockwise order where needed. Round one skips Production.

Round structure

Production: Collect resources from your Starting Location and from your current Location if you have an Embassy there. Put a Collection token on each other Embassy Location to show it may be collected later in Command. A Location can be collected only once each round; three Embassies there produce double.
Discovery: Beginning with the first player, each player at the map edge places up to two tiles adjacent to their current Location (up to three in a two-player game). Take only as many as can legally be placed. Recruiting Locations offer crew, resources, and Embassies; Anomalies instead have their printed effects.
Sensor: Each player rolls two Sensor dice and resolves the result. With two reward faces, choose one; with two blanks, optionally reroll one die. One Encounter icon draws one Encounter, while two let you draw two and choose one. Once per round, spend one Influence to reroll a Sensor die.
Command: In any order, and as often as resources and available Crew permit, move, recruit, build Embassies, complete Expeditions, collect marked Locations, and spend resources or Influence. Each Ship has one normal move; each Warp Jump costs two Raw Materials or one Crystal for one extra move.



Teaching priorities

Build an Embassy only while your Ship is at that Recruiting Location and you can pay its printed cost. The first Embassy gives its Location card, level-one Crew, and one Influence; the second gives level-two Crew; the third gives level-three Crew and one point. New Crew enters Transit and is available next round.
You may build one Embassy at another player’s non-starting Location, but do not receive its Location or Crew. Both players still produce its full resources.
Complete as many Expeditions as you can meet. Play the required Crew to Transit, score the card’s points, and take its bonus if its extra requirement is also met. At round end, replace completed regular Expeditions until you have three non-secret ones, choosing any difficulty.
Crew skill, level, Embassy, and Location Expeditions have different requirements. Used Crew cannot complete another Expedition or Encounter that round. Secret Expeditions cost three Influence, stay hidden, and are not replaced.
Spend two Raw Materials on an Upgrade, place it in the next Dashboard slot, and refill the six-card store. Influence can also replace an Expedition, add a Location beside your current location, trade resources 2:1 for the round, reroll a Sensor die, or buy a Secret Expedition.



Player variants
The rulebook’s solo game uses a Nameless drone and its own movement/action decks. Optional modules, including objectives and events, change scoring or round procedures and are not part of this base-game teach.

title: Stellar Expedition
text:
Scoring
There is no separate final scoring phase. Expedition points are earned when Expeditions are completed and when a third Embassy is built on a Recruiting Location. After the eighth round ends, total those points.

Endgame

After all players finish the round-eight Command phase, return Transit Crew, move Sickbay and Solo Mission Crew to Transit, retrieve unused Collection tokens, and advance the Gate marker as usual.
Add Expedition points from completed Expeditions and from Locations where you built three Embassies.
The highest total wins. Ties go first to the highest combined Crew levels, then to the most Location cards; any remaining tie is shared.

title: Stellar Expedition
text:
Terminology

Gate: The central starting point and the eight-round timer’s theme.
Nameless: The ancient aliens associated with the Gate; their drone appears only in solo play.
Crew: Cards with skills and levels, recruited through Embassies and committed to Expeditions or Encounters.
Embassy: A cube on a Recruiting Location that unlocks crew, production, and Influence.
Expedition Point: The victory-point currency, chiefly earned from Expeditions and completed three-Embassy Locations.

title: Agropolis
text:
Work together to turn 15 landscape cards into a productive farm and meet three revealed scoring conditions.



Agropolis is a cooperative game for 1-4 players.
Discuss placement freely, but never show cards in hand. Once a player reveals a chosen card, it must be placed.

title: Agropolis
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Shuffle all 18 cards and set three aside scoring-condition side up. Add their numbers: this is the target score.
Choose a start player. Deal that player three cards, block side down, and each other player one card, also block side down.
Put the remaining cards to one side, block side up, as the draw deck. Put its top card face up in the build area to begin the map.
The start player takes the first turn; play proceeds clockwise.

title: Agropolis
text:
Rounds and Phases

A placement turn

Choose one of your cards, reveal its block side, and add it to the map.
Pass every card still in your hand to the player on your left. They become the active player.
Draw the top card of the draw deck, if any, so you hold one card. When you have fewer than two cards to pass, pass what remains after your turn.
Continue until all 15 non-scoring cards have been added.



Placement constraints

Place every card horizontally; it may be rotated 180 degrees but not otherwise rotated or flipped.
A new card must either have a block edge touching an existing block edge or cover one or more existing blocks.
Never tuck a card under another card and never join the map only at a corner. Gaps are allowed if these rules are met.



Farm planning

A block is one rectangular quarter of a card. The four types are cornfield, orchard, vineyard, and livestock.
A group is matching blocks connected by at least one edge. Build large groups, but inspect the three scoring conditions before committing space.
A road is a continuous stretch of roadway. Keeping roads together reduces the final penalty.

title: Agropolis
text:
Scoring
When the fifteenth map card is placed, score as follows:

Score one point for every block in your largest group of each of the four types. For a tie, choose one tied largest group.
Subtract one point for every separate road.
Add or subtract the result of each revealed scoring condition.
Win if the final total equals or exceeds the target score; otherwise the team loses.


Feed Fees
Feed Fees are an optional harder-game rule. For every matching livestock symbol beneath the three selected scoring conditions, add one to the target score. A game can have more than one fee.

title: Agropolis
text:
Terminology

Block: one rectangular zone on a card.
Group: matching blocks joined edge-to-edge.
Road: a continuous roadway, from one block to the map edge or across several blocks.
Scoring condition: one of the three set-aside cards; its number contributes to the target and its text modifies scoring.

Rounds and Phases

Play a level
There is no turn order. Any player may place their lowest-feeling card face-up in the centre. Continue until every dealt card is in one ascending shared pile.


When a card is too high
If a player reveals a card while another player still holds a lower card:

Lose one shared life.
Every player discards all cards lower than the card just played.
Continue the same level with the cards that remain.



Throwing stars and level rewards
At any agreed moment, a player may raise a hand to ask for a throwing star. If everyone agrees, spend one: every player discards their lowest hand card face-up. After completing a level, discard remaining used cards, reveal the next level, and award any life or star shown on that level card before dealing again.

title: The Mind
text:
Scoring

Win or lose together
The game has no points. Clear the final level to win. The instant the team loses its last life, the game ends in a shared loss. There is no tiebreak because the team has one result.

Terminology

Key terms

Level: a round with a specified number of cards per player.
Life: a shared error allowance.
Throwing star: a shared aid that discards everyone’s lowest card.
Shared pile: cards played in ascending order.

title: Sprawlopolis
text:
Work together to build a city from 15 cards that meets three changing civic demands.



Sprawlopolis is cooperative for 1-4 players.
Table talk is encouraged, but do not show cards in hand. A card must be placed after its owner chooses and reveals it.

title: Sprawlopolis
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Shuffle the 18 cards and set three aside scoring-condition side up. Their numbers added together are the target score.
Choose a start player. Deal them three block-side-down cards and deal every other player one block-side-down card.
Make a block-side-up draw deck from the remaining cards. Place its top card face up in the build area to start the city.
The start player begins; turns proceed clockwise.

title: Sprawlopolis
text:
Rounds and Phases

A placement turn

Choose and reveal one card from your hand, then add it to the city.
Pass all cards remaining in hand to the player on your left. They take the next turn.
Draw one card from the deck, if possible, so you have one card to pass. If fewer than two cards remain in hand when it is time to pass, pass those remaining cards.
Stop when all 15 city cards have been placed.



Placement constraints

Place cards horizontally and rotate them only 180 degrees; do not flip them.
A card must have at least one block edge meeting an existing block edge, or overlap and cover one or more blocks.
Do not tuck a card under another, and a corner-only connection is illegal. Open spaces are allowed.



City-building priorities

A block is a rectangular quarter of a card: commercial, park, industrial, or residential.
A group is matching blocks joined by an edge. Make large groups while accommodating the scoring conditions.
A road is a continuous roadway. Separate roads each cost a point.

title: Sprawlopolis
text:
Scoring
After the final card is placed:

Score one point per block in the largest group of each zone type. If tied groups are largest, choose one.
Subtract one point for every road.
Apply the positive or negative result of all three scoring conditions.
The team wins if its final score equals or exceeds the target; otherwise it loses.

For an easier game, ignore road penalties. For a harder game, score only the largest group of one zone type.

title: Sprawlopolis
text:
Terminology

Block: one rectangular zone on a card.
Group: matching blocks connected edge-to-edge.
Road: a continuous roadway, from one block to the city edge or across several blocks.
Scoring condition: one of the three set-aside cards; its number sets part of the target and its text changes final scoring.

title: Turing Machine
text:
Turing Machine is a deduction game for 1-4 players. Everyone investigates the same unique three-digit code, composed of one number from 1-5 in each of three colours. Be the first to identify the code that passes every verifier’s hidden criterion.


Each verifier checks exactly one criterion, selected from the possibilities on its Criteria card. A verification result says only whether the current proposal passes that criterion; it does not directly reveal the answer code or the criterion itself. Every verifier is necessary and no verifier duplicates another’s information.

title: Turing Machine
text:

Each verifier checks exactly one criterion, selected from the possibilities on its Criteria card. A verification result says only whether the current proposal passes that criterion; it does not directly reveal the answer code or the criterion itself. Every verifier is necessary and no verifier duplicates another’s information.

title: Turing Machine
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Prepare a problem

Place the Machine tile centrally and assemble the punch-card support. Sort the punch cards in the support by number, with all 1s first, then all 2s, and so on.
Choose one printed problem. Problems 1-16 are introductory. Its entry specifies the verifiers, their Criteria cards, and the matching Verification cards.
Put each specified Criteria card before its verifier and its Verification card face down beside it. Mark each Verification card’s back with its verifier letter to prevent mix-ups. Cross out unused verifier columns on every note sheet.
Give every player a player aid and note sheet. The player aids screen private notes; proposals and the verifiers chosen are public, but answers and deductions are secret.

title: Turing Machine
text:
Rounds and Phases

Make and test a proposal
All players perform each round simultaneously:

Compose: overlay three differently coloured punch cards to make a single three-digit proposal, then record it on the current round of the note sheet.
Question: test that unchanged proposal with up to three verifiers, or fewer if preferred. Slide each chosen verifier’s Verification card beneath the aligned punch cards and record its pass or fail result in the matching verifier column. Return the card face down to its verifier immediately.
Deduce: return the punch cards to the support, analyse the results, and update private deductions. Recording every proposal and every result is compulsory because questions break ties.
End the round: all players simultaneously indicate whether they think they have found the code. If nobody does, begin another round.



Read a verifier correctly
The hole visible through the aligned cards shows a pass or fail for that proposal against one criterion. Keep the same proposal for every question in the round. A pass proves only that the proposal meets a possible criterion, not that any tested digit is part of the answer. If a needed punch card is temporarily in use, wait until the other player has finished with it.


Solo, cooperative, and handicap play
Solo or cooperative players use one note sheet and try to solve the chosen problem in as few rounds and questions as possible, still asking at most three questions each round. To handicap an experienced competitive player, pre-fill one or two answer spaces on that player’s first-round sheet; each counts as a question already used.

title: Turing Machine
text:
Scoring

Verify and end the game
When one or more players declare, each secretly writes a proposed code, then checks it against the problem solution. A correct declaration must also be demonstrable by composing that code and showing it passes every verifier.
If several players are correct, the player who asked the fewest questions wins; equal totals share the win. Incorrect declarers are eliminated and the remaining players continue. If that leaves one player, that player wins by default.

title: Turing Machine
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Code: the unique three-colour, three-digit solution.
Proposal: a three-digit combination submitted to verifiers during one round.
Verifier: the machine component that checks one hidden criterion.
Criteria card: the public list of possible criteria for a verifier.
Verification card: the face-down card used with punch cards to show pass or fail.
Punch card: one coloured number card used to construct a proposal.
Question: one consultation of one verifier; at most three per round.

title: The Old King’s Crown
text:
In this 2-4 player game, lead one of four factions vying to replace the old king. Accumulate Influence over a fixed number of years by bidding for useful Kingdom cards, committing forces to three regions, and winning their clashes. Influence in your supply, rather than territorial control, wins the crown.



A Faction card can bid, occupy a Kingdom card, fight in a region, supply votes to a Council, or be sent on a Journey for Lore. Each use closes off the others.
You secretly place one card at each region before Summer, then can reinforce, retreat, move, or eliminate cards through Actions, Commands, and effects.
Heralds choose the exact location whose reward you hope to claim; Supporters add strength to a region’s first clash. Neither stays on the map indefinitely.

title: The Old King’s Crown
text:

Accumulate Influence over a fixed number of years by bidding for useful Kingdom cards, committing forces to three regions, and winning their clashes. Influence in your supply, rather than territorial control, wins the crown.



A Faction card can bid, occupy a Kingdom card, fight in a region, supply votes to a Council, or be sent on a Journey for Lore. Each use closes off the others.

Heralds choose the exact location whose reward you hope to claim; Supporters add strength to a region’s first clash. Neither stays on the map indefinitely.

title: The Old King’s Crown
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Choose the standard five-round game (recommended), or a four-round short game or six-round extended game. Put the round marker on 1, the season marker on Spring, and stack the three clash markers I, II, III with I on top.
Put the Kingdom board and Councils tile in reach. Shuffle the Kingdom deck onto the Great Road, fill its three spaces from right to left with face-up cards, then reveal the top deck card: four Kingdom cards are available. Make a common reserve of Influence and Lore, and put the Kingdom’s Favour on the Harvest Field.
Each player chooses a faction and takes its board, Herald, five Supporters, four unexhausted Tactics, markers, Site of Power, and hand-size marker at its printed starting value. Put that faction’s advanced cards and HQ cards face-up at its Site of Power.
Find the faction’s Heir, put it in hand, shuffle the remaining basic Faction cards into its deck, and draw to six cards. Determine starting order by age or randomly; the first player takes the active-player marker.

title: The Old King’s Crown
text:
Rounds and Phases
The game has five phases per round. Resolve simultaneous steps together; resolve turn-order steps from the top of the Order track down. Actions are optional and normally usable once per round; mandatory effects resolve simultaneously in their indicated effects step. Card text overrides the general rules.

Start of the year
Skip this phase in round 1. Everyone draws up to hand size, then reorder players by Influence in supply, highest first. A tie reverses the tied players’ previous order. If you must draw from an empty deck, shuffle your discard pile into a new deck, reduce hand size by one, and draw to the new size; hand size cannot fall below three or rise above eight.


Spring: bid, commit, and prepare

Everyone secretly places one Faction card as a bid, then reveals. Bid strength is the card’s Strength plus effects that modify bids; ignore its other attributes unless an effect says otherwise. Resolve bids from highest strength down, breaking ties by Order track.
On resolving a bid, either take a face-up Great Road Kingdom card and occupy it with the bidding card, steal an opponent’s occupied Kingdom card if your bid is strictly stronger than its occupying card, or return your bidding card to hand. You may have only two occupied Kingdom cards; replacing one discards its Kingdom card and returns its former occupying card to hand.
Refresh the Great Road. If cards were taken from it, discard its rightmost remaining card, slide the rest right, refill from the deck, then reveal the top deck card. If none were taken, discard the two rightmost cards first. A card removed from the Road outside bidding is simply replaced, without that discard.
In turn order, each player places their Herald on any location. Then everyone secretly places one card from hand next to each of the three regions. Those cards remain private until their region’s clash.
In turn order, each player may use any available Spring Actions and Commands, including placing any number of Supporters from their board into regions. Each Supporter adds 1 strength only in that region’s first clash this round.



Summer: resolve the three clashes
The last player on the Order track assigns clash markers I-III to the regions, setting the resolution order. For each region:

Reveal all cards there. Face-up cards next to a region are Active.
In turn order, players use any available Day Actions and Commands. An Active card may Ambush a further face-down card into the clash; reveal new cards after everyone has acted, then only Actions and Commands on those newly revealed cards may be used in another turn-order pass.
Resolve all mandatory Night effects simultaneously. Deadly eliminates opponents’ Active cards in the clash; Invulnerable cards cannot be eliminated, while Resilient cards go to their owner’s discard instead of the Lost Pile.
Total each player’s strength: unused Active-card strength in that region, +1 for each unused Supporter there, plus modifiers. Highest total wins. If tied players all pass when offered the choice to add a face-down card, the region is tied and nobody receives rewards; otherwise begin a new clash among the tied players. Cards and Supporters used in an earlier clash in that region do not count in the new one.
The winner chooses either location in that region. If their Herald is there, they gain 1 Influence and steal 1 Influence, if possible, from each opponent Herald there. Then take the location’s printed Influence and may take its additional reward. A resolved region cannot clash again that round.



Autumn and Winter
In Autumn, each player acts in turn order and may interleave any number of available Actions/Commands with one Govern and one Journey. Govern moves a hand card with at least one vote to a chosen Council. Journey moves a hand card with Lore to the Lost Pile and gains Lore equal to its icons; when you gain Lore, you may immediately spend any amount of Lore to acquire advanced cards to hand or HQ cards to supply from your Site of Power.
In Winter, resolve mandatory effects, then clean up simultaneously: return Heralds to player boards, move map Supporters to the Lost Pile, return clash markers, and discard remaining Active cards with no Influence on them. For an Active card bearing Influence, remove one Influence instead. Advance the round marker; after the selected final round, end the game.

title: The Old King’s Crown
text:
Scoring

Winning the crown
After the final round, first convert Lore to Influence if your Site of Power is empty: gain 1 Influence for every 2 Lore in supply. Then the player with the most Influence in supply wins. A tie goes first to a tied player holding the Kingdom’s Favour; if none does, the tied player highest on the Order track wins.


Key exception
The Kingdom’s Favour is claimed whenever a player takes the Harvest Field’s location reward, even if another player holds it. It provides the holder’s faction-specific Action and begins with three uses; rotate it after each use and return it to the Harvest Field after the third. Reclaiming it resets it to three uses. Holding it is also the first endgame tie-breaker.

title: The Old King’s Crown
text:
Terminology

Influence: The victory currency. Keep it in your supply; the most at game end wins.
Lore: Currency gained chiefly by Journeying and spent only when you gain Lore, to acquire Site of Power cards.
Herald / Supporter: A Herald occupies one location for potential reward; a Supporter occupies a whole region and adds 1 strength to its first clash.
Kingdom card: A shared Great Road card that must normally be occupied by the Faction card used to bid for it.
Active card: A face-up Faction card next to a region.
Clash: The Summer contest in one region. The winner chooses one of its two locations for rewards.
Lost Pile: The public shared pile for eliminated cards, Journey cards, and spent Supporters.

title: Mysterium
text:
One player is the Ghost, communicating only through surreal vision cards. The psychics must interpret those visions to reconstruct the murder and identify the culprit.


The Ghost knows every answer but may not explain, gesture, or react to guesses. Psychics may discuss their theories freely, but must make their own final choices. Treat the Ghost’s visions as associative clues, not literal evidence.

title: Mysterium
text:
One player is the Ghost, communicating only through surreal vision cards. The psychics must interpret those visions to reconstruct the murder and identify the culprit.


The Ghost knows every answer but may not explain, gesture, or react to guesses. Psychics may discuss their theories freely, but must make their own final choices. Treat the Ghost’s visions as associative clues, not literal evidence.

title: Mysterium
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Prepare the investigation

Choose one player as the Ghost; everyone else is a psychic.
Use the player-count setup on the Ghost screen to lay out the required character, location, and object cards.
Give each psychic an intuition token and sleeve. For 4-7 players, also give a clairvoyancy marker at 0 and four tokens at 4-5 players or six at 6-7; 2-3 players do not use clairvoyancy.
Choose difficulty and lay out the required number of each card type: Easy 4/5/5/6/6/7, Medium 5/6/6/7/8/8, Hard 6/7/7/8/9/9 for 2-7 players. Give the Ghost the correspondingly numbered ghost cards, who secretly assigns one character, location and object to each psychic.
Set the clock to hour 1. The Ghost draws seven vision cards and takes crows according to difficulty: one discard per turn at Easy, three per game at Medium, or one per game at Hard.

The Ghost must keep each psychic’s solution secret. Psychics should see only the public suspect displays and their own tokens.

title: Mysterium
text:
Rounds and Phases

Each of the seven hours

Each unresolved psychic is on character, then location, then object, in that order. The Ghost gives each at least one vision card, marks that psychic as served, and redraws to seven after each vision; the Ghost may not speak, gesture or otherwise signal.
Start the two-minute timer. Psychics may discuss and move their intuition tokens until it expires; more than one may choose the same public card.
Before time expires, a psychic may put one agree or disagree clairvoyancy token on another psychic’s intuition token, never their own. Tokens are discarded after use and returned at the start of hour four.
The Ghost reveals each result. A correct psychic discards their visions, puts the correct card in their sleeve, and advances to the next category. An incorrect psychic keeps their visions and remains on that category, receiving additional visions in later hours.
Successful clairvoyancy predictions advance their owners one space. A psychic completing all three cards moves to the mission space and gains one clairvoyancy space per hour remaining, but keeps helping and may spend remaining tokens. Advance the clock.



Ghost tools and final phase
The group loses if anybody remains unresolved when hour seven ends. Otherwise, make one numbered group from each completed character-location-object set. The Ghost secretly chooses the culprit group, selects three vision cards, one pointing to each element of that group, shuffles them face-down as the shared vision, and records its group number.
Reveal the shared vision one card at a time. Psychics vote secretly for a group when their clairvoyancy level permits them to see one, two, or all three cards; they may not discuss the vote. Reveal votes when all have voted. The group with most votes is chosen; a tie goes to the choice of the furthest clairvoyant, then the eldest player if still tied. For 2-3 players, each player runs two psychics, no clairvoyancy is used, three shared visions are face-up, two random extra groups bring the total to four, and the psychics agree openly on a vote.

title: Mysterium
text:
Scoring

Win or lose together
Mysterium has no individual score. The group loses if all psychics have not completed their three-card combinations within seven hours, or if its final selected group is not the Ghost’s culprit. It wins only if the final group is correct. Clairvoyancy determines how much of the shared vision a psychic sees, not points.

title: Mysterium
text:
Terminology

Key terms

Ghost: gives vision cards but never explains their meaning.
Psychic: an investigator interpreting visions.
Vision card: an illustrated, associative clue.
Hour: one timed investigation round.
Intuition token: marks a psychic’s current guess.
Clairvoyancy: predictions of others’ guesses that unlock more shared-vision cards for the final vote.
Crow: lets the Ghost cycle unhelpful vision cards.
Culprit: the correct completed solution in the final vote.

title: Oceans
text:
Evolve marine species in a connected ecosystem. Feed your species, adapt to rivals, and finish with the most points.



Oceans supports 2-4 players in this supplied quick-rules guide.
Each player maintains their own species, but every feeding and attack changes a shared food web.

title: Oceans
text:
Evolve marine species in a connected ecosystem. Feed your species, adapt to rivals, and finish with the most points.



Oceans supports 2-4 players in this supplied quick-rules guide.
Each player maintains their own species, but every feeding and attack changes a shared food web.

title: Oceans
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Prepare the ecosystem

Put the Reef and three Ocean Zones together; shuffle Scenario cards and put one beneath Zones 1 and 2. Put the Cambrian Explosion card, Reef Variant face-down, in Zone 1. For a gentler beginner game, use the Reef Variant and do not use Deep cards.
Deal six Surface cards to each player. Shuffle the Deep deck and reveal two cards as the Gene Pool. Set aside 60 population in reserve, then distribute 100/120/140 population among the Reef and three Ocean Zones for 2/3/4 players.
Reveal and discard the top Surface card; move its migration number from both the Reef and Zone 1 into Zone 3. Give players screens and choose a first player. Award end-game point tokens: 4/0 for 2 players, 6/4/0 for 3, or 7/6/4/0 for 4.



What you are building

A species board holds its population as fish and its trait cards.
Traits can help a species feed, defend itself, attack, migrate, or change other rules.
Keep your hand behind the player screen unless a card instructs otherwise.

title: Oceans
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take a turn
Take the following four phases, then pass play clockwise.

Playing Cards: before the Cambrian Explosion, play one Surface card; after it, play any two cards one at a time. Each card either evolves a species or migrates population. To evolve, start a new species or add the card beside an existing one; a species normally has at most three traits, but there is no species limit. Traits are active immediately and may be removed during this phase. To migrate, discard a card and move up to its migration number from one water zone to one other water zone.
Feeding: choose one species to forage from the Reef or attack one species, including your own. It must have an empty space and be able to take at least one population. Use total green forage or red attack value, defaulting to one if no value is shown; the defender’s shell value saves that many population. Take the full possible amount, subject to board capacity. Resolve all triggered traits, then overpopulation: a species with population on its fishbone space falls to five and returns the excess to one water zone.
Aging: move one population from each species to your score pile, or two after the Cambrian Explosion. A species goes extinct only if it cannot remove the full required aging amount: score what remains, then remove its board and traits.
Drawing Cards: optionally take one Deep card, either from the Gene Pool or by drawing three and keeping one, putting the other two face-up on the Gene Pool. Discard any number of Surface cards, then draw Surface cards to a hand of six.



Surface and Deep

The Cambrian Explosion occurs when Zone 1 first empties, even if population later returns. From then on, play two cards, age two population, and Deep traits may be played.
A Deep card played as a trait costs population from the player’s score pile equal to its migration number, returned to one water zone. A Deep card used for migration costs nothing but is removed from the game. Deep cards are not used in the Reef Variant.
A blue Scenario remains active while its corresponding empty zone remains empty; a purple Scenario resolves each time that zone empties. Resolve trait triggers and overpopulation before the Scenario.



End-of-round care
The game continues until all three Ocean Zones are empty. Then put the 60 reserve population into Zone 3 and continue only until the last player in turn order, the player with the zero-point token, finishes their turn. Population and species boards are unlimited; use substitutes if needed after the end-game trigger.

title: Oceans
text:
Scoring

End of game
At game end, score:

population in your score pile behind the screen;
population currently on species boards; and
the setup point token.

The highest total wins; ties go to the player with the most traits currently in play.

title: Oceans
text:
Terminology

Species: one of your evolving animals.
Population: fish on a species board.
Surface trait: a card used to evolve a species or discarded to migrate.
Deep trait: a unique trait, playable after the Cambrian Explosion by paying scored population.
Reef / Ocean: the shared fish supplies from which population and effects draw.
Extinction: removal during Aging when a species cannot pay its full aging amount.

text:
Official rules

title: Evolution: Climate
text:
Evolution: Climate supports 2-6 players. Feed species, adapt them to predators and temperature, and preserve population for final scoring. Food eaten is banked as points; surviving population and traits score too.



Food cards jointly determine both plant food and whether climate moves one zone warmer or colder.
The climate can reduce population before anyone feeds; protective traits stack where applicable.
A hungry carnivore feeds only through legal attacks, while non-carnivores normally use the Watering Hole.

title: Evolution: Climate
text:
Evolution: Climate supports 2-6 players. Feed species, adapt them to predators and temperature, and preserve population for final scoring. Food eaten is banked as points; surviving population and traits score too.



Food cards jointly determine both plant food and whether climate moves one zone warmer or colder.
The climate can reduce population before anyone feeds; protective traits stack where applicable.
A hungry carnivore feeds only through legal attacks, while non-carnivores normally use the Watering Hole.

title: Evolution: Climate
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?
Use the 2-3 player side of the climate board for 2-3 players and the 4-6 player side otherwise. Put the marker in Temperate, make the Food Bank, give each player a food bag, shuffle the trait deck, and deal no starting hand. Reveal one cold and one hot Climate Event under the named zones, then randomly choose the first player.

Table checklist

Remove and set aside roughly 88 trait cards for 2 players, 60 for 3, 30 for 4, and none for 5-6. The set-aside cards become the replacement draw deck in smaller games.
Each player begins their first Deal Cards phase with one Species board at population 1 and body size 1.
Use the 2-player exception of at most three traits per species. Six players use the Quick Play variant, in which all players play Phase 3 simultaneously.

title: Evolution: Climate
text:
Rounds and Phases
The game normally lasts five to seven rounds. Each round has five phases: Deal Cards, Select Food Cards, Play Cards, Modify Environment, and Feeding.

Round sequence

Deal Cards: give each player four cards plus one per existing species. If the deck runs out now, or ran out during an extinction in the prior round, this is the final round. Rebuild it from the discard pile in 5-6 players or the set-aside cards in 2-4 players.
Select Food Cards: everyone secretly chooses one hand card for the Watering Hole.
Play Cards: starting with first player, each player may add face-down non-duplicate traits to species (maximum four), discard cards to create a new size-1/population-1 species at either end of their row, or discard to increase one species’ body size or population by one, up to six. Reveal new traits after everyone has played. A player may also discard an existing trait during their turn and may cycle hand cards to the bottom of the deck after playing; replacement cards cannot be played until next round.
Modify Environment: first resolve pre-reveal leafy-frame traits; reveal food cards; shift climate one zone toward the majority of Sun or Snowflake icons; resolve an event in the current zone; apply climate population loss; add or remove plant food from the total food-card value adjusted by the climate zone; then replace a triggered event. Only one event can trigger per round.
Feeding: starting with first player and cycling clockwise, each player must feed one hungry species until all are fed or none can eat. A non-carnivore takes one plant food from the Watering Hole. A hungry carnivore instead attacks a species, including its own, only if it has greater body size and bypasses every defence; reduce prey population by one, then take meat equal to the prey’s body size. Carnivores never eat plant food.



Feeding reminders

A species is hungry for every population without food, and normally cannot eat above population. At feeding end, lose all hungry population; population zero is extinct.
Put food from species boards into owners’ bags after feeding; remaining Watering Hole plant food stays for the next round.
On extinction, discard its traits, draw one card per discarded trait, bank its food, discard the species board, and close any gap in its row.
If the game continues, pass first player left. Climate Event cards are optional for a first game, but this teach otherwise assumes they are used.

title: Evolution: Climate
text:
Scoring
After the final round’s Feeding phase, score 1 point per food token in your bag, plus the population of every surviving species, plus 1 per trait on surviving species. Highest score wins; then compare trait-card points, then population points. If still tied, play again as the rulebook directs.

Final round
Running out of the draw deck does not end the game immediately: create the replacement deck if needed, finish the current round, and then score. An extinction that exhausts the deck makes the next round the final round.

title: Evolution: Climate
text:
Terminology

Species: A board with population, body size, and up to four traits (three in 2 players).
Food card: The secretly chosen trait card determining food and climate pressure.
Watering Hole: The shared supply of plant food.
Climate Event: The currently exposed hot- or cold-side effect in a climate zone.
Hungry: A species with fewer food tokens than required by its population.

title: Fluxx
text:
Fluxx is a card game whose rules and victory condition change during play. Put the right Keepers in front of you when the current Goal appears.

title: Fluxx
section: Setting up: How to get started?
text:
Setting up: How to get started?

Deal the game

Shuffle all cards into one deck.
Deal three cards to each player.
Make a face-down draw pile and leave room for discards.
Choose a first player by any fair method.
Begin with no Keepers, no Goal, and only Draw 1, Play 1.

If the draw pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile into a new draw pile. Never shuffle cards that remain in play.

title: Fluxx
text:
Rounds and Phases

Take a turn

Draw the number of cards required by the active Draw rule.
Play the number required by the active Play rule.
Resolve each card immediately. A Goal or New Rule replaces the existing card of that type.
After playing, obey every active Hand Limit and Keeper Limit by discarding excess cards of your choice.
Check the current Goal before play passes clockwise.



What each card does

Keepers stay face-up in front of their owner.
Goals set the current win condition. With no Goal, nobody wins normally.
New Rules take effect immediately and can alter this turn.
Actions resolve once, then go to the discard pile.

If you must play more cards than you hold, play all you can. When rules conflict, the newest relevant card wins; a card’s specific instruction overrides the general rules.

title: Fluxx
text:
Scoring

End of the game
There is no points total. The instant a player has all Keepers listed on the current Goal, that player wins, including during another player’s Action or rule change. If several players meet it at once, they all win.

title: Fluxx
text:
Terminology

Card types and limits

Keeper: a card kept face-up in front of a player.
Goal: the current winning requirement.
New Rule: a card that changes how the game is played.
Action: a one-off instruction, resolved and then discarded.
Hand Limit: maximum cards held after a turn.
Keeper Limit: maximum Keepers kept after a turn.

title: Towards a general framework for co-location
text: Previous studies into co-location exist in a variety of fields such as epidemiology and human mobility. In each field, researchers are interested identifying points of co-location amongst members of a population. In each of these fields, however, the definition of what it means for members of the population to be co-located may differ; furthermore, the ways in which data are collected vary. This piece of work aims to provide an initial outline of a general framework for identifying points of co-location. It demonstrates that the identification of co-location points between individuals is sensitive to the way in which co-location is defined in each context, as well as the types of data used. Furthermore, it highlights the impact that uncertainty in observations can have on our ability to reliably identify co-location.

title: Simplifying the interpretation of continuous time models for spatio-temporal networks
text: Autoregressive and moving average models for temporally dynamic networks treat time as a series of discrete steps which assumes even intervals between data measurements and can introduce bias if this assumption is not met. Using real and simulated data from the London Underground network, this paper illustrates the use of continuous time multilevel models to capture temporal trajectories of edge proper ties without the need for simultaneous measurements, along with two methods for producing interpretable summaries of model results. These including extracting ‘features’ of temporal patterns (e.g. maxima, time of maxima) which have utility in understanding the network properties of each connection and summarising whole-network properties as a continuous function of time which allows estimation of network properties at any time without temporal aggregation of non-simultaneous measurements. Results for temporal pattern features in the response variable were captured with reasonable accuracy. Variation in the temporal pattern features for the exposure variable was underestimated by the models. The models showed some lack of precision. Both model summaries provided clear ‘real-world’ interpretations and could be applied to data from a range of spatio-temporal network structures (e.g. rivers, social networks). These models should be tested more extensively in a range of scenarios, with potential improvements such as random effects in the exposure variable dimension.

title: An agent-based model of heterogeneous driver behaviour and its impact on energy consumption and costs in urban space
text: By 2020, over 100 countries had expanded electric and plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (EV/PHEV) technologies, with global sales surpassing 7 million units. Governments are adopting cleaner vehicle technologies due to the proven environmental and health implications of internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs), as evidenced by the recent COP26 meeting. This article proposes an agent-based model of vehicle activity as a tool for quantifying energy consumption by simulating a fleet of EV/PHEVs within an urban street network at various spatio-temporal resolutions. Driver behaviour plays a significant role in energy consumption; thus, simulating various levels of individual behaviour and enhancing heterogeneity should provide more accurate results of potential energy demand in cities. The study found that (1) energy consumption is lowest when speed limit adherence increases (low variance in behaviour) and is highest when acceleration/deceleration patterns vary (high variance in behaviour); (2) vehicles that travel for shorter distances while abiding by speed limit rules are more energy efficient compared to those that speed and travel for longer; and (3) on average, for tested vehicles, EV/PHEVs were £233.13 cheaper to run than ICEVs across all experiment conditions. The difference in the average fuel costs (electricity and petrol) shrinks at the vehicle level as driver behaviour is less varied (more homogeneous). This research should allow policymakers to quantify the demand for energy and subsequent fuel costs in cities.

title: Coupling an agent-based model and an ensemble Kalman filter for real-time crowd modelling
text: Agent-based modelling has emerged as a powerful tool for modelling systems that are driven by discrete, heterogeneous individuals and has proven particularly popular in the realm of pedestrian simulation. However, real-time agent-based simulations face the challenge that they will diverge from the real system over time. This paper addresses this challenge by integrating the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) with an agent-based crowd model to enhance its accuracy in real time. Using the example of Grand Central Station in New York, we demonstrate how our approach can update the state of an agent-based model in real time, aligning it with the evolution of the actual system. The findings reveal that the EnKF can substantially improve the accuracy of agent-based pedestrian simulations by assimilating data as they evolve. This approach not only offers efficiency advantages over existing methods but also presents a more realistic representation of a complex environment than most previous attempts. The potential applications of this method span the management of public spaces under ‘normality’ to exceptional circumstances such as disaster response, marking a significant advancement for real-time agent-based modelling applications.
